title: Tracking Spending
text:
1 Book Topics

Tracking vs. budgeting: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop
Capture methods: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month
Categorizing: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use “Other”, and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row
Using spreadsheets: bank exports have Date, Description, and Amount columns; a keyword lookup adds the Category column in one pass
Monthly review: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick one change for next month
Online subscriptions: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days
Math: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700)

title: Tracking Spending
text:
3 Categorizing Transactions
A bank export only says where the money went (Description). Adding a Category column turns a list of merchants into budget buckets. In R, dplyr::case_when() checks each rule in order and the first match wins; in Python, numpy.select() does the same with a list of conditions and a list of labels; in Excel, IFS() does it one cell at a time. Anything that matches no rule falls into “Other”.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks so grocery stores (Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods, Costco) become “Groceries” and everything without a rule becomes “Other”. How many transactions are groceries?

ExcelPythonR


With Description in column B, write an IFS() formula in D2 that labels subscriptions, groceries, and “Other”, then fill it down and count the groceries.






NoteSolution





SEARCH() finds a keyword in a cell, ISNUMBER() turns that into true/false, and OR() joins several keywords. The final TRUE, "Other" catches everything else.
=IFS(
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Netflix",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Spotify",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("NYTimes",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("24 Hour Fitness",B2))), "Subscriptions",
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Trader Joe",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Whole Foods",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Costco",B2))), "Groceries",
  TRUE, "Other"
)







IFS() in Excel


Then count them with =COUNTIF(D:D, "Groceries"). The answer is 3.

















Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The default label is "Other".


desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco")],
    ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum()


















Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The last rule’s label is "Other".


statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Groceries") |>
  nrow()









3.2 Level 2: Practice
Next month’s export has three new merchants: Safeway (groceries), Hulu (a subscription), and Uber (transportation). The rules below don’t know them yet, so they land in “Other”. Update the rules so no transaction is left in “Other”.

ExcelPythonR


Your IFS() formula labels the new month’s Safeway, Hulu, and Uber rows as “Other”. Edit it so =COUNTIF(D:D, "Other") returns 0.






NoteSolution





Add each new merchant to its group with another ISNUMBER(SEARCH(...)) inside the OR(), and add a Transportation rule:
OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Safeway",B2))), "Groceries",
OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Hulu",B2))), "Subscriptions",
OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Shell",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Uber",B2))), "Transportation",
Re-fill the formula down after editing it.

















Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".


desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Payroll"),
     desc.str.contains("Rent"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway"),
     desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu"),
     desc.str.contains("Shell|Uber"),
     desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")],
    ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Other").sum()


















Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".


statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income",
    grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Shell|Uber", Description) ~ "Transportation",
    grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Other") |>
  nrow()









3.3 Level 3: Challenge
Real bank exports are messy: the same merchant can show up as NETFLIX.COM, Netflix, or netflix. The rule below only matches the exact capitalization, so it finds just 1 of the 3 subscriptions. Change the code so capitalization doesn’t matter, and count the subscriptions again.

ExcelPythonR


Does the IFS() and SEARCH() formula need any change for NETFLIX.COM?






NoteSolution





No. SEARCH() ignores capitalization, so SEARCH("Netflix", "NETFLIX.COM") already finds a match. (Its case-sensitive cousin is FIND().)

















str.contains() has a case argument. Look at what case=False does.


is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", case=False)
is_sub.sum()


















grepl() has an ignore.case argument.


messy |>
  filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description, ignore.case = TRUE)) |>
  nrow()

title: Tracking Spending
text:
4 Answering Tracking Questions
Once every row has a category, the book’s three tracking questions take one short pipeline each: what did subscriptions cost, what share of income went to fixed costs, and which variable category was biggest? Spending is stored as negative numbers, so a minus sign turns a spending total positive.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
What did the four subscriptions cost this month?

ExcelPythonR


With Amount in C and Category in D, total the subscriptions as a positive number.






NoteSolution





=-SUMIF(D:D, "Subscriptions", C:C)
This returns $83.97.

















Pick the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".


-statement.loc[statement["Category"] == "Subscriptions", "Amount"].sum()


















Keep the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".


statement |>
  filter(Category == "Subscriptions") |>
  summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  pull(total)









4.2 Level 2: Practice
Fixed costs are housing, utilities, and insurance. What share of income went to fixed costs? Give the answer as a decimal (for example, 0.25 for 25%).

ExcelPythonR


Total the three fixed categories and divide by income (the positive amounts).






NoteSolution





=-(SUMIF(D:D,"Housing",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Utilities",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Insurance",C:C))/SUMIF(C:C,">0")
This returns 0.803, or about 80%.

















statement["Category"].isin(fixed) picks the fixed-cost rows. Sum their Amount and flip the sign.


fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"]
income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total = -statement.loc[statement["Category"].isin(fixed), "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total / income


















filter(Category %in% fixed) keeps the fixed-cost rows; then summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) and pull(total).


fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance")
income <- statement |> filter(Amount > 0) |> pull(Amount) |> sum()
fixed_total <- statement |> filter(Category %in% fixed) |> summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |> pull(total)
fixed_total / income









4.3 Level 3: Challenge
Leaving out income, fixed costs, and subscriptions, which category had the most spending? Return its name.

ExcelPythonR


Find the biggest variable category without scrolling through the rows.






NoteSolution





Select the data and use Insert → PivotTable with Category in Rows and Amount in Values, then sort smallest to largest (spending is negative). Or list the variable categories in F2:F4 (Groceries, Transportation, Dining), total each in G2 with =-SUMIF(D:D, F2, C:C), fill down, and use:
=INDEX(F2:F4, MATCH(MAX(G2:G4), G2:G4, 0))
The answer is Groceries ($303.35).

















Filter out the skip categories with ~statement["Category"].isin(skip), then groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum(). Spending is negative, so the biggest is .idxmin().


skip = ["Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions"]
variable = statement[~statement["Category"].isin(skip)]
variable.groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum().idxmin()


















filter(!Category %in% skip), then group_by(Category) and summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)). Finish with slice_max(Total, n = 1) and pull(Category).


skip <- c("Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions")
statement |>
  filter(!Category %in% skip) |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  slice_max(Total, n = 1) |>
  pull(Category)

title: Tracking Spending
text:
5 The Subscription Audit Math
A $20/month subscription feels trivial. Cancel it and invest the $240 a year instead, and the chart below shows what that money grows into at each checkpoint, split into the money you put in and the growth it earned.
Formula: Annual cost × ((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r = Opportunity cost in n years
With the book’s 7% real return (the return after inflation), r = 0.07.





$240 a year invested at 7% instead of a $20/month subscription







$240 a year invested at 7% instead of a $20/month subscription




Each bar adds another year’s $240 to everything saved so far, and the whole pile grows by 7%. After 30 years you put in $7,200, and growth added about $15,500.

5.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish subscription_opportunity_cost(), then find what a $20/month subscription costs over 30 years at 7%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the monthly cost in A2 (20), the years in B2 (30), and the return in C2 (0.07). In D2, write the opportunity cost.






NoteSolution





=(A2*12)*((1+C2)^B2-1)/C2
A2*12 turns the monthly cost into a yearly one. =FV(C2, B2, -A2*12) gives the same $22,670.59.







Opportunity Cost in Excel
















A year has 12 monthly payments. The growth factor is raised to the number of years.


def subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, years, rate=0.07):
    annual_cost = monthly_cost * 12
    return annual_cost * ((1 + rate) ** years - 1) / rate

subscription_opportunity_cost(20, 30)















A year has 12 monthly payments. The growth factor is raised to the number of years.


subscription_opportunity_cost <- function(monthly_cost, years, rate = 0.07) {
  annual_cost <- monthly_cost * 12
  annual_cost * ((1 + rate)^years - 1) / rate
}
subscription_opportunity_cost(20, 30)









5.2 Level 2: Practice
Audit all four subscriptions from the bank statement (Netflix $15.99, Spotify $10.99, NYTimes $17.00, 24 Hour Fitness $39.99). What is their combined opportunity cost over 30 years?

ExcelPythonR


List the four monthly costs in A2:A5, keep 30 and 0.07 in B and C, fill the D2 formula down, and total the column.






NoteSolution





=SUM(D2:D5)
This returns $95,182.47. The gym membership alone is $45,330 of it.

















The function works on a whole column at once: pass subs["monthly"] and 30.


subs["after_30"] = subscription_opportunity_cost(subs["monthly"], 30)
subs["after_30"].sum()


















The function is vectorized: pass the whole monthly column and 30.


subs |>
  mutate(after_30 = subscription_opportunity_cost(monthly, 30)) |>
  summarise(total = sum(after_30)) |>
  pull(total)









5.3 Level 3: Challenge
The audit formula adds money once a year. Subscriptions are really paid monthly. Write monthly_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, years, rate = 0.07) that invests every month (use a monthly rate and the number of months), then price the survey’s $219/month over 30 years.

ExcelPythonR


Find the 30-year value of $219 invested every month at 7%.






NoteSolution





=FV(7%/12, 30*12, -219)
This returns $267,173.65, about $12,000 more than yearly deposits because each month’s money starts growing sooner.














Use monthly_rate = rate / 12 and periods = years * 12, then the same formula with monthly_cost in place of the yearly amount.


def monthly_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, years, rate=0.07):
    monthly_rate = rate / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return monthly_cost * ((1 + monthly_rate) ** periods - 1) / monthly_rate

monthly_opportunity_cost(219, 30)















Use monthly_rate <- rate / 12 and periods <- years * 12, then the same formula with monthly_cost in place of the yearly amount.


monthly_opportunity_cost <- function(monthly_cost, years, rate = 0.07) {
  monthly_rate <- rate / 12
  periods      <- years * 12
  monthly_cost * ((1 + monthly_rate)^periods - 1) / monthly_rate
}
monthly_opportunity_cost(219, 30)

title: Savings Strategies
text:
1 Book Topics

Savings rate: the one number to track; it sets the speed of wealth building more than income does (a $40,000 earner saving 40% reaches $500k in 18 years, a $120,000 earner saving 10% takes 21)
Benchmarks: under 10% danger zone; 10 to 20% average; 20 to 30% strong; 30%+ path to financial independence within a decade or two
Make savings automatic: automate transfers the day after payday, use a separate bank, label each account by purpose, and track progress visually
Savings and the FOO: saving shows up at nearly every step of the Financial Order of Operations; the right rate is the one you can keep up for decades
Account types: high yield savings and money market accounts for emergency and sinking funds, CDs for known future goals, regular savings to avoid
FDIC insurance: covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank; spread larger balances across banks

title: Savings Strategies
text:
2 Savings Rate
The savings rate is the slice of your income bar that goes to savings. Every dollar goes to either spending or savings, so the rate measures how big the savings slice is.
Formula: Savings Rate = (Income − Spending) ÷ Income × 100
Example: you take home $5,000 and spend $3,500. (5,000 − 3,500) ÷ 5,000 = 30% savings rate.





Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)







Savings slice as a percentage of income (same $60k income, different rates)




How to read this result: a 30% rate means 30 cents of every dollar you bring home stays with you. If the rate is negative, you are spending more than you earn and the gap is coming from savings or debt.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish savings_rate(), then find the savings rate when you take home $5,000 and spend $3,500.

ExcelPythonR


Put income in A2 (5000) and spending in B2 (3500). Find the savings rate in C2.






NoteSolution





=(A2 - B2) / A2 * 100
This returns 30.














What you save is what you earn minus what you spend.


def savings_rate(income, spending):
    return ((income - spending) / income) * 100

savings_rate(5000, 3500)















What you save is what you earn minus what you spend.


savings_rate <- function(income, spending) {
  ((income - spending) / income) * 100
}
savings_rate(5000, 3500)









2.2 Level 2: Practice
Flip the formula. To save 25% of a $5,000 paycheck, what is the most you can spend? Spending = Income × (1 − Rate).

ExcelPythonR


Put income in A2 (5000) and the target rate in B2 (0.25). Find the spending limit in C2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * (1 - B2)
This returns $3,750.














Write 25% as 0.25. The share you can spend is 1 - target_rate.


def spending_limit(income, target_rate):
    return income * (1 - target_rate)

spending_limit(5000, 0.25)















Write 25% as 0.25. The share you can spend is 1 - target_rate.


spending_limit <- function(income, target_rate) {
  income * (1 - target_rate)
}
spending_limit(5000, 0.25)









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
Label each spending level on a $5,000 income with the book’s tier: under 10% is “Danger zone”, 10% to under 20% “Average”, 20% to under 30% “Strong”, and 30% or more “FI path”. Spending levels: $4,700, $4,250, $3,750, $3,250, and $5,200.

ExcelPythonR


Put spending in A2:A6, the rate in B2:B6, and the tier in C2:C6.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =(5000-A2)/5000*100. In C2, filled down:
=IFS(B2 < 10, "Danger zone", B2 < 20, "Average", B2 < 30, "Strong", TRUE, "FI path")
The tiers are Danger zone, Average, Strong, FI path, Danger zone. The last one spends more than it earns (-4%).

















np.select() checks conditions in order: [rate < 10, rate < 20, rate < 30] with labels ["Danger zone", "Average", "Strong"] and default="FI path". Finish with .tolist().


levels["rate"] = savings_rate(5000, levels["spending"])
rate = levels["rate"]
levels["tier"] = np.select(
    [rate < 10, rate < 20, rate < 30],
    ["Danger zone", "Average", "Strong"],
    default="FI path"
)
levels["tier"].tolist()


















case_when() checks in order: rate < 10 ~ "Danger zone", then rate < 20, then rate < 30, then .default = "FI path". Finish with pull(tier).


levels |>
  mutate(
    rate = savings_rate(5000, spending),
    tier = case_when(
      rate < 10 ~ "Danger zone",
      rate < 20 ~ "Average",
      rate < 30 ~ "Strong",
      .default = "FI path"
    )
  ) |>
  pull(tier)

title: Savings Strategies
text:
3 Years to a Savings Target
The book compares two savers at a 7% return. One earns $40,000 and saves 40% ($16,000 a year). The other earns $120,000 and saves 10% ($12,000 a year). The bigger saver reaches $500,000 first. We can solve for the number of years directly.
Formula: Years = ln(1 + Target × r ÷ Annual Savings) ÷ ln(1 + r)
Example: ln(1 + 500,000 × 0.07 ÷ 16,000) ÷ ln(1.07) = 17.1 years, so the balance passes $500k during year 18. At $12,000 a year it takes 20.2 years, so year 21.





Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income







Years to reach $500,000 at a 7% return on a $60,000 income




How to read this result: the answer is the number of years of steady saving needed, not counting anything you already have. Raising the savings rate shortens the timeline much more at low rates than at high ones.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish years_to_target(), then find how long $16,000 a year at 7% takes to reach $500,000.

ExcelPythonR


Put yearly savings in A2 (16000), the target in B2 (500000), and the return in C2 (0.07). Find the years in D2.






NoteSolution





=NPER(C2, -A2, 0, B2)
This returns about 17.1 years.














The formula is ln(1 + Target × r ÷ Annual Savings) ÷ ln(1 + r).


import math
def years_to_target(annual_savings, target, rate=0.07):
    return math.log(1 + target * rate / annual_savings) / math.log(1 + rate)

years_to_target(16000, 500000)















The formula is ln(1 + Target × r ÷ Annual Savings) ÷ ln(1 + r).


years_to_target <- function(annual_savings, target, rate = 0.07) {
  log(1 + target * rate / annual_savings) / log(1 + rate)
}
years_to_target(16000, 500000)









3.2 Level 2: Practice
A higher earner saves $12,000 a year (10% of $120,000). In which year does the balance pass $500,000?

ExcelPythonR


Change A2 to 12000 and round up.






NoteSolution





=ROUNDUP(NPER(C2, -A2, 0, B2), 0)
This returns 21, four years after the $40,000 earner saving 40%.

















Round up with math.ceil(); the balance passes the target during that year.


math.ceil(years_to_target(12000, 500000))

R uses <- (preferred convention) or = for assignment.


Python Uses = for assignment.






x <- 10


x = 10









R Functions are created with function() and assigned to a variable. Function bodies are wrapped in curly braces {}.


Python Functions are defined with the def keyword, followed by a colon and an indented body.






add_fun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}


def add_fun(a, b):
    return a + b









R automatically returns the last evaluated expression. The return() function is optional.


Python requires an explicit return statement to return a value—otherwise returns None.






double_fun <- function(x) x * 2


def double_fun(x):
    return x * 2









R has a built-in pipe |> (base R) and the popular %>% operator from magrittr/dplyr for chaining operations.


Python has no native pipe operator. Chaining is done via method calls—polars is especially well-suited for this style.






data |>
  filter(x > 5) |>
  summarise(avg = mean(x))


import polars as pl

(
    data
    .filter(pl.col("x") > 5)
    .select(pl.col("x").mean().alias("avg"))
)









R uses paste(), paste0(), sprintf(), or glue::glue() for string construction.


Python uses f-strings, the .format() method, or % formatting.






name <- "John"
paste0("Hello, ", name)
glue::glue("Hello, {name}")


name = "John"
f"Hello, {name}"









R uses curly braces {} to define code blocks. Indentation is purely stylistic.


Python uses indentation (typically 4 spaces) to define code blocks. Indentation is syntactically required.

  print("positive")
}


if x > 0:
    print("positive")









Spaces, line breaks, and indentation are flexible and stylistic in R


In Python, indentation is syntactic (inconsistent indentation raises an IndentationError). Blank lines are ignored but can be used to separate code blocks for readability.






# R — all of this is valid 
# and produces the same result

# Clean, conventional style

  result <- x * 2
  print(result)
}

# Messy but still valid
if(x>0){result<-x*2
    print(result)}

# Extreme and ugly but works

result        <-x*2
   print(   result   )
              }


# Python — indentation matters
# Correct: consistent 4-space 
# indentation

    result = x * 2
    print(result)

# Blank lines are fine 
# they improve readability

    if x > 0:
        result = x * 2

        print(result)

    return result

# Raises IndentationError
if x > 0:
    result = x * 2
        print(result) # ❌ bad indent









R uses 1-based indexing.


Python uses 0-based indexing.






vec <- c("a", "b", "c")
vec[1]   # returns "a"


lst = ["a", "b", "c"]
lst[0]   # returns "a"









R uses NA (with variants like NA_integer_, NA_character_), plus NULL and NaN.


Python uses None natively; polars represents missing values as null in its columnar data structures.






x <- c(1, NA, 3)
is.na(x)


import polars as pl
s = pl.Series([1, None, 3])
s.is_null()









In R, vectors are first-class citizens—most operations are vectorized by default.


In Python, native lists are not vectorized. Vector math requires numpy or columnar libraries like polars.






c(1, 2, 3) * 2   
# returns c(2, 4, 6)


import polars as pl
pl.Series([1, 2, 3]) * 2   
# returns Series [2, 4, 6]









In R, packages are installed with install.packages() and loaded with library().


In Python, packages are installed via pip or conda from the terminal and loaded with import.






install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


# terminal: pip install polars
import polars as pl









In R, comments are single-line only, using #. No multi-line comment syntax.


In Python, single-line comments use #. Triple-quoted strings ("""...""") are commonly used as block comments or docstrings.






# This is a comment


# This is a comment

"""
This is a multi-line
comment or docstring.
"""









In R, TRUE / FALSE (can be abbreviated as T / F).


In Python, True / False (capitalized, no abbreviation).






flag <- TRUE


flag = True






R uses &, |, ! for vectorized logic; &&, || for scalar logic.
c(TRUE, FALSE) & c(TRUE, TRUE)   # vectorized
TRUE && FALSE                    # scalar
Python uses and, or, not for scalar logic; &, |, ~ for vectorized logic in numpy/polars expressions.
True and False  # scalar

import polars as pl
df.filter((pl.col("a") > 0) & (pl.col("b") < 10)) # vectorized



data.frame is built into base R; enhanced versions include tibble (tidyverse) and data.table.
df <- data.frame(
    name = c("A", "B"), 
    value = c(1, 2)
  )
In Python, data frames are not built-in—requires a library like polars (pl.DataFrame), which offers fast, multithreaded performance and a clean expression API.
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["A", "B"], "value": [1, 2]})

title: Major Purchases
text:
1 Book Topics

Renting vs. buying: “renting is throwing money away” is a myth; you pay for shelter either way, and Ben Felix’s research shows renting and investing the difference often matches or beats owning
True cost of owning: mortgage interest, property tax (1% to 2%), maintenance (about 1%), insurance, closing costs (3% to 5%), and the opportunity cost of the down payment
Felix’s 5% rule: unrecoverable costs run about 5% of home value per year (property tax ~1% + maintenance ~1% + cost of capital ~3%); divide by 12 and compare to rent
When to buy or rent: buy if you’ll stay 7+ years, have stable income and an emergency fund, and keep housing under 28% to 30% of gross income; rent if you may move within 5 to 7 years or need flexibility; a decision flowchart ties it together
Front loaded interest: on a 30 year mortgage at 6%, more than 80% of the first year’s payments go to interest, so moving every 5 years means barely touching principal

title: Major Purchases
text:
2 The Rent-vs-Buy 5% Rule
The 5% rule adds up three costs every owner pays and never gets back. Divide by 12 and you have a monthly rent to compare against.
Formula: Monthly cost of owning ≈ (Home Value × 0.05) ÷ 12





The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home







The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home




Example: a $500,000 home → (500,000 × 0.05) ÷ 12 = $2,083 a month. Rent below that, and renting and investing the difference tends to win.
How to read this result: the threshold is the rent at which renting and owning cost about the same. It’s a quick filter, not a final answer; your plans to stay and your local rents still matter.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish rent_buy_threshold(), then find the 5% rule’s monthly cost of owning a $500,000 home.

ExcelPythonR


Put the home value in A2 (500000) and the rate in B2 (0.05). Find the monthly threshold in C2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * B2 / 12
This returns $2,083.33.














5% of the home’s value is lost each year; divide by 12 for a month.


def rent_buy_threshold(home_value, unrecoverable_rate=0.05):
    return (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12

rent_buy_threshold(500000)















5% of the home’s value is lost each year; divide by 12 for a month.


rent_buy_threshold <- function(home_value, unrecoverable_rate = 0.05) {
  (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12
}
rent_buy_threshold(500000)

3 The Monthly Mortgage Payment
The standard amortization formula spreads the loan plus all future interest into equal monthly payments. Shorter terms mean higher payments but far less total interest.
Formula: M = P × [r(1 + r)^n] ÷ [(1 + r)^n − 1], where P = loan principal, r = annual rate ÷ 12, n = years × 12





Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms







Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms




Example: a $480,000 loan (a $600,000 home with 20% down) at 6% for 30 years → about $2,878 a month.
How to read this result: the monthly payment is only part of the cost. Before choosing a term, check that the payment plus property tax and insurance stays under 28% to 30% of gross income.

Find the payment in one formula.






NoteSolution





=PMT(6%/12, 360, -480000)
This returns $2,877.84.














Mortgages are paid monthly: a monthly rate and a number of months.


def mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * (r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, 30)















Mortgages are paid monthly: a monthly rate and a number of months.


mortgage_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}
mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, 30)

4 Where the First Year’s Payments Go
In month one, interest is the balance times the monthly rate. Only what’s left over reduces the principal.
Formula: First month interest = Principal × (annual rate ÷ 12); First month principal = Monthly payment − First month interest





Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage







Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage




Example: on that $480,000 loan, month one interest is $2,400 of the $2,878 payment, about 83% interest, leaving only about $478 toward principal.
How to read this result: early on, your payment mostly rents money from the bank. Equity builds slowly at first and quickly at the end, so selling within a few years leaves little principal paid down.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
In month one of the $480,000 loan at 6%, interest is the balance × (6% ÷ 12). Fill in the blanks to find how much of the $2,877.84 payment actually pays down the loan.

ExcelPythonR

=A2 - B2
Interest is $2,400, so only $477.84 goes to principal.

















The monthly rate is 0.06 / 12. Principal is whatever is left of the payment after interest.


payment = mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, 30)
interest = 480000 * (0.06 / 12)
payment - interest

This returns 83.4.

Build a 60-row schedule with month, starting balance, interest, principal, and ending balance, then total the principal.

Or skip the table: =-CUMPRINC(6%/12, 360, 480000, 1, 60, 0) returns $33,339.09, about 7% of the loan.

balance = 480000

    balance -= payment - balance * 0.005

480000 - balance

title: Insurance
text:
1 Book Topics

The rule: insure losses you can’t absorb; cover small ones from your emergency fund (leave room for error)
Insurance words: premium, deductible, claim, coverage limit, liability; premiums and deductibles move in opposite directions
Health insurance: never go without; stay on a parent’s plan until 26, get it through work, or use the marketplace; copay, coinsurance, and the out of pocket maximum (your worst case, capped at $10,600 in 2026); high deductible plans qualify for an HSA with a deductible of at least $1,700 and an out of pocket maximum of no more than $8,500
Auto insurance: liability of at least 100/300/100; consider dropping collision and comprehensive on a cheap car
Renters insurance: about $13 to $23 a month; choose replacement cost over actual cash value
Disability insurance: about 1 in 4 of today’s 20 year olds will become disabled before retirement age; take employer long term disability (about 60% of pay)
Life insurance: only if someone depends on your income; buy term, about 10 times yearly income; skip whole life
Umbrella insurance: $1 million or more of extra liability; revisit as net worth grows
What to skip: extended warranties, phone insurance, life insurance with no dependents, single event policies

title: Insurance
text:
2 Choosing a Deductible
A higher deductible lowers your premium but costs more on each claim. The break even point is how many years of premium savings it takes to cover the extra deductible.
Formula: Break even years = (Higher deductible − Lower deductible) ÷ Yearly premium savings





Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year







Savings from a $1,000 deductible vs. a $500 deductible, year by year




Car insurance costs $1,500 a year with a $500 deductible, or $1,350 with a $1,000 deductible. ($1,000 − $500) ÷ $150 = about 3.3 years. If you file a claim less often than that, the higher deductible comes out ahead.
How to read this result: a positive yearly gain means the higher deductible saves money on average. The gain turns negative only if you claim more often than the break even. Either way, pick the higher deductible only if your emergency fund can cover it.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish break_even_years(), then find how many claim-free years it takes for a $1,000 deductible (instead of $500) that saves $150 a year to pay off.

ExcelPythonR


Put the higher deductible in A2 (1000), the lower one in B2 (500), and the yearly savings in C2 (150). Find the break-even years in D2.






NoteSolution





=(A2 - B2) / C2
This returns 3.3 years.














The extra risk you take on is the difference between the two deductibles.


def break_even_years(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings):
    return (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings

break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)















The extra risk you take on is the difference between the two deductibles.


break_even_years <- function(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings) {
  (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings
}
break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)









2.2 Level 2: Practice
Another quote: a $2,000 deductible instead of $500 saves $250 a year. What is the break-even?

ExcelPythonR


Change the inputs to 2000, 500, and 250.






NoteSolution





The same formula returns 6 years.

















High 2000, low 500, savings 250.


break_even_years(2000, 500, 250)


















High 2000, low 500, savings 250.


break_even_years(2000, 500, 250)









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
Back to the $1,000 vs. $500 choice that saves $150 a year. If you file one claim every k years, your yearly gain from the higher deductible is 150 − 500 ÷ k. Of k = 2, 3, 5, and 10, what is the most frequent claim rate (smallest k) where the higher deductible comes out ahead?

ExcelPythonR


Put k in A2:A5, the yearly gain in B, and find the smallest k with a positive gain.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =150 - 500/A2. Then:
=MINIFS(A2:A5, B2:B5, ">0")
The answer is 5. Claiming every 2 or 3 years, the lower deductible is cheaper.

claim_every = [2, 3, 5, 10]
min(k for k in claim_every if 150 - 500 / k > 0)

min(claim_every[gain > 0])

title: Insurance
text:
3 Comparing Two Health Plans
A health plan’s real yearly cost is its premiums plus your share of medical bills, minus any money your employer puts in your HSA. Your share can never go above the out of pocket maximum.
Formula: Yearly cost = (Monthly premium × 12) + min(Medical bills, Out of pocket max) − Employer HSA money
This simple version assumes you pay all medical bills up to the out of pocket maximum, so it slightly overstates plans with coinsurance.





Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year







Total yearly cost of two health plans in a healthy year and the worst year




Plan A has a $100 monthly premium and a $3,000 out of pocket maximum. Plan B has a $40 monthly premium, a $5,000 out of pocket maximum, and $500 a year from your employer in the HSA. In a healthy year ($300 of care), Plan A costs $1,500 and Plan B costs $280. In the worst year, Plan A costs $4,200 and Plan B costs $4,980.





Yearly cost of each plan as medical bills grow







Yearly cost of each plan as medical bills grow




How to read this result: the gap between the lines is what you save (or lose) with Plan B. Below $4,220 of bills, Plan B wins by up to $1,220. Above it, Plan A wins by at most $780. If you put Plan B’s savings into the HSA, one healthy year covers the difference.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish plan_cost(), then find Plan A’s yearly cost ($100 a month, $3,000 out-of-pocket max) in a healthy year with $300 of medical bills.

ExcelPythonR


Put the premium in A2 (100), bills in B2 (300), the out-of-pocket max in C2 (3000), and employer HSA money in D2 (0). Find the yearly cost in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2*12 + MIN(B2, C2) - D2
This returns $1,500.














Premiums are paid every month. You never pay more in bills than the out-of-pocket max.


import numpy as np
def plan_cost(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa=0):
    return monthly_premium * 12 + np.minimum(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa

plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)















Premiums are paid every month. You never pay more in bills than the out-of-pocket max.


plan_cost <- function(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa = 0) {
  monthly_premium * 12 + pmin(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa
}
plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)









3.2 Level 2: Practice
Plan B costs $40 a month with a $5,000 out-of-pocket max, and the employer puts $500 in your HSA. What does Plan B cost in the worst year, when you hit the max?

ExcelPythonR


Change the inputs to 40, a very large bill (or the max), 5000, and 500.






NoteSolution





=40*12 + 5000 - 500
This returns $4,980, versus $4,200 for Plan A.

















A bill of infinity means you hit the out-of-pocket max. The max is 5000 and the HSA money is 500.


plan_cost(40, float("inf"), 5000, employer_hsa=500)


















A bill of Inf means you hit the out-of-pocket max. The max is 5000 and the HSA money is 500.


plan_cost(40, Inf, 5000, employer_hsa = 500)









3.3 Level 3: Challenge
Plan B is cheaper in healthy years and Plan A in bad ones. Checking medical bills from $3,000 to $5,000 in $10 steps, what is the lowest bill where Plan B costs as much as or more than Plan A?

ExcelPythonR


Work it out with algebra: above $3,000, Plan A is capped at 1,200 + 3,000, and Plan B is 480 + bills − 500.






NoteSolution





Set them equal: 480 + bills − 500 = 4,200, so =4200 - 480 + 500 gives $4,220.

















plan_cost() uses np.minimum, so it works on the whole bills array. Compute a and b, then bills[b >= a].min().


bills = np.arange(3000, 5001, 10)
a = plan_cost(100, bills, 3000)
b = plan_cost(40, bills, 5000, employer_hsa=500)
bills[b >= a].min()


















plan_cost() uses pmin(), so it works on all bills at once. Compute a and b, then min(bills[b >= a]).


bills <- seq(3000, 5000, by = 10)
a <- plan_cost(100, bills, 3000)
b <- plan_cost(40, bills, 5000, employer_hsa = 500)
min(bills[b >= a])

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
1 Book Topics

Separate account: the real benefit of a savings account at a different bank is friction; 1 to 2 days to move money back stops impulse spending
Choosing an account: need it within 6 months? Use a HYSA. Can you lock it away for 3 to 60 months? Consider a CD
Comparing HYSAs: online banks pay about 4 to 5% APY and differ by only 0.1 to 0.4%; all of them beat the 0.01% at traditional banks by about 400×
APY vs. APR: APY already includes daily compounding, so balance growth is Starting Balance × (1 + APY)^years
FDIC insurance: covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank; money market accounts are a close alternative with possible withdrawal limits
Savings hierarchy: emergency fund, sinking funds, and short term goals go in a HYSA; 3 to 5 year goals in CDs or short term bonds; 5+ years goes to investing

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
2 HYSA Balance
APY is the total return for a year with compounding already included. To grow a balance, multiply by (1 + APY) once for each year you hold the money.
Formula: Ending Balance = Starting Balance × (1 + APY)^years
(The daily math belongs to the APR: APY = (1 + APR ÷ 365)^365 − 1.)
Example: $10,000 at 4.35% APY grows to $10,000 × 1.0435 = $10,435 after one year ($435 in interest) and to $12,373 after five years.





$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year







$10,000 at 4.35% APY: deposit and interest earned, year by year




How to read this result: the green layer is money the bank paid you. On $10,000 the gap between online banks is about $20 a year, but the gap between any of them and a traditional bank is over $400.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish hysa_balance(), then find what $10,000 grows to after one year at 4.35% APY.

ExcelPythonR


Put the deposit in A2 (10000), the APY in B2 (0.0435), and years in C2 (1). Find the balance in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * (1 + B2)^C2
This returns $10,435.














The APY already includes compounding, so grow by (1 + annual_apy) once per year.


def hysa_balance(principal, annual_apy, years=1):
    return principal * (1 + annual_apy) ** years

hysa_balance(10000, 0.0435)















The APY already includes compounding, so grow by (1 + annual_apy) once per year.


hysa_balance <- function(principal, annual_apy, years = 1) {
  principal * (1 + annual_apy)^years
}
hysa_balance(10000, 0.0435)









2.2 Level 2: Practice
Leave the same $10,000 alone for 5 years. What is the balance?

ExcelPythonR


Change C2 to 5.






NoteSolution





The same formula returns $12,372.64.

















Pass the deposit, the APY, and years=5.


hysa_balance(10000, 0.0435, years=5)


















Pass the deposit, the APY, and years = 5.


hysa_balance(10000, 0.0435, years = 5)









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
Compare one year on $10,000 at four banks: Regular bank 0.01%, Ally 4.20%, Discover 4.35%, and Amex 4.40%. How much more interest does the best bank pay than the worst?

ExcelPythonR


Put the banks in A2:A5 and APYs in B2:B5. Find each year’s interest in C, then the gap.






NoteSolution





In C2, filled down: =10000*B2. Then:
=MAX(C2:C5) - MIN(C2:C5)
This returns $439 ($440 vs. $1).

















banks["interest"] = hysa_balance(10000, banks["apy"]) - 10000, then .max() - .min() on that column.


banks["interest"] = hysa_balance(10000, banks["apy"]) - 10000
banks["interest"].max() - banks["interest"].min()


















mutate(interest = hysa_balance(10000, apy) - 10000), then summarise(gap = max(interest) - min(interest)) and pull(gap).


banks |>
  mutate(interest = hysa_balance(10000, apy) - 10000) |>
  summarise(gap = max(interest) - min(interest)) |>
  pull(gap)

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
3 Small Rate Gaps Over Time
The book says a 0.3% difference looks like noise at first but adds up over 30 years of regular deposits. To check, we need the growth of a monthly deposit, using the monthly rate that matches the APY.
Formula: Future Value = Deposit × ((1 + i)^(12 × years) − 1) ÷ i, where i = (1 + APY)^(1/12) − 1
Example: $500 a month for 30 years grows to about $342,635 at 4.0% APY and $360,801 at 4.3% APY, a gap of about $18,166.





$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs







$500 a month for 30 years at three APYs




How to read this result: the gap is small for the first few years and grows with time. It is worth picking a good rate once, but not worth switching banks every month to chase 0.05%.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish hysa_deposits_fv(), then find what $500 a month grows to in 30 years at 4.0% APY.

ExcelPythonR


Put the deposit in A2 (500), the APY in B2 (0.04), and years in C2 (30). Find the balance in D2.






NoteSolution





=FV((1+B2)^(1/12)-1, 12*C2, -A2)
This returns $342,635.28.














Turn the APY into a monthly rate with the 12th root, then compound once per month.


def hysa_deposits_fv(monthly_deposit, annual_apy, years):
    i = (1 + annual_apy) ** (1 / 12) - 1
    return monthly_deposit * ((1 + i) ** (12 * years) - 1) / i

hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, 30)















Turn the APY into a monthly rate with the 12th root, then compound once per month.


hysa_deposits_fv <- function(monthly_deposit, annual_apy, years) {
  i <- (1 + annual_apy)^(1 / 12) - 1
  monthly_deposit * ((1 + i)^(12 * years) - 1) / i
}
hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, 30)









3.2 Level 2: Practice
Another bank pays 4.3% instead of 4.0%. Over the same 30 years of $500 deposits, how much bigger is the balance?

ExcelPythonR


Add the 4.3% row and find the gap.






NoteSolution





=FV(1.043^(1/12)-1, 360, -500) - FV(1.04^(1/12)-1, 360, -500)
This returns $18,165.86.

















Same deposit and years, APY 0.043.


hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.043, 30) - hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, 30)


















Same deposit and years, APY 0.043.


hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.043, 30) - hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, 30)









3.3 Level 3: Challenge
Small gaps take time to matter. Of the horizons 5, 10, 20, and 30 years, which is the first where the 4.3% account is ahead by more than $5,000?

ExcelPythonR


Put the horizons in A2:A5, the gap for each in B2:B5, and find the first above $5,000.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =FV(1.043^(1/12)-1, 12*A2, -500) - FV(1.04^(1/12)-1, 12*A2, -500). Then:
=INDEX(A2:A5, MATCH(TRUE, B2:B5>5000, 0))
The answer is 20 years ($6,018). At 10 years the gap is only $1,128.

















Compute the gap with both APYs for each horizon, then use next(y for y in horizons if ...) or a loop with break.


horizons = [5, 10, 20, 30]
next(y for y in horizons if hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.043, y) - hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, y) > 5000)


















The function is vectorized: compute both balances for all horizons, subtract, and use min(horizons[...]).


horizons <- c(5, 10, 20, 30)
gap <- hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.043, horizons) - hysa_deposits_fv(500, 0.04, horizons)
min(horizons[gap > 5000])

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts
text:
4 FDIC Coverage
FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per account holder per bank. Anything above that at one bank is not insured.
Formula: Insured = smaller of (Balance, $250,000); Uninsured = Balance − Insured; Banks Needed = Balance ÷ $250,000, rounded up
Example: a $10,000 balance is fully insured. A $500,000 balance at one bank has $250,000 uninsured, so it needs two banks.
How to read this result: if the uninsured column is above zero, move that amount to an account at a different bank.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor per bank. Fill in the blanks to find the uninsured part of $500,000 at one bank.

ExcelPythonR


Put the balance in A2 (500000). Find the insured amount in B2 and the uninsured amount in C2.






NoteSolution





=MIN(A2, 250000)
=A2 - B2
$250,000 is uninsured.














Insured is the smaller of the balance and the limit.


balance = 500000
insured = min(balance, 250000)
balance - insured















Insured is the smaller of the balance and the limit.


balance <- 500000
insured <- min(balance, 250000)
balance - insured









4.2 Level 2: Practice
How many banks do you need to fully insure $610,000?

ExcelPythonR


Put the balance in A2 (610000). Find the banks needed.






NoteSolution





=ROUNDUP(A2 / 250000, 0)
This returns 3.














Divide by the limit and round up; 2.44 banks means you need 3.


import math
math.ceil(610000 / 250000)















Divide by the limit and round up; 2.44 banks means you need 3.


ceiling(610000 / 250000)









4.3 Level 3: Challenge
Four savers each keep everything at one bank: $10,000, $250,000, $500,000, and $610,000. How much money is uninsured in total?

ExcelPythonR


Put the balances in A2:A5, the uninsured amount in B2:B5, and total it.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =A2 - MIN(A2, 250000). Then =SUM(B2:B5) returns $610,000.

















savers["balance"].clip(upper=250000) caps every balance at the limit.


savers["insured"] = savers["balance"].clip(upper=250000)
savers["uninsured"] = savers["balance"] - savers["insured"]
savers["uninsured"].sum()


















min() returns one number for the whole column. pmin(balance, 250000) works row by row.


savers |>
  mutate(
    insured   = pmin(balance, 250000),
    uninsured = balance - insured
  ) |>
  summarise(total = sum(uninsured)) |>
  pull(total)

title: Estate Planning
text:
1 Book Topics

Why it matters young: at 18 your parents lose the right to act for you; set up a plan while you’re thinking clearly, since people tend to miss their own cognitive decline
Beneficiary designations: the ten minute task; name a primary and contingent beneficiary on retirement plans, IRAs, HSAs, life insurance, and bank (POD) and brokerage (TOD) accounts; these forms override your will
Financial power of attorney: a durable POA names an agent to handle your money if you can’t
Healthcare directive and HIPAA release: a healthcare proxy and living will (often one advance directive), plus a HIPAA form so doctors can share information
Will and trust: a will covers what has no beneficiary, names an executor, and names a guardian for children; without one, state intestate succession decides; most people starting out don’t need a trust
Paperwork and parents: store originals safely, keep an account list (no passwords), set up password manager emergency access, and ask your parents about their plan

title: Estate Planning
section: 2 What You Own and What You Owe
text:
2 What You Own and What You Owe
Your estate starts with your net worth: everything you own minus everything you owe.
Formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total debts





Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old







Assets, debts, and net worth for a 25 year old




Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $8,000 + $9,000) − ($6,000 + $1,000) = $35,000 − $7,000 = a net worth of $28,000.
How to read this result: net worth is the yearly check in on your progress. It’s also roughly what your estate would be worth today, before adding any life insurance.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish net_worth(), then find the net worth for assets of $12,000 (401(k)), $6,000 (Roth IRA), $8,000 (savings), and $9,000 (car), with debts of $6,000 (car loan) and $1,000 (credit card).

ExcelPythonR


Put the assets in B2:B5 and the debts in B7:B8. Find net worth in B10.






NoteSolution





=SUM(B2:B5) - SUM(B7:B8)
This returns $28,000.














Add up everything you own, then everything you owe.


def net_worth(assets, debts):
    return sum(assets) - sum(debts)

net_worth([12000, 6000, 8000, 9000], [6000, 1000])















Add up everything you own, then everything you owe.


net_worth <- function(assets, debts) {
  sum(assets) - sum(debts)
}
net_worth(c(12000, 6000, 8000, 9000), c(6000, 1000))

A recent graduate has $3,000 in savings, a $5,000 car, and $30,000 of student loans. What is their net worth?

Put the new numbers in the sheet.

net_worth([3000, 5000], [30000])

title: Estate Planning
section: 3 How Much Your Beneficiary Forms Control
text:
3 How Much Your Beneficiary Forms Control
Life insurance isn’t part of net worth while you’re alive, but it pays out when you die. Add it, then split the estate by what decides who gets each piece.
Formula: Share controlled by beneficiary forms = Assets with a named beneficiary ÷ Total estate





What decides who gets each part of the estate







What decides who gets each part of the estate




Example: ($12,000 + $6,000 + $45,000 + $8,000) ÷ $80,000 = about 89% of the estate, decided by forms that take minutes to fill out. That’s why beneficiary designations come before a will for most young people.
How to read this result: the higher the share, the less your will has to do. With every form filled in, a will only decides the car. With no forms, all $80,000 goes through probate.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish beneficiary_share(), then find the share of an $80,000 estate controlled by beneficiary forms when the 401(k) ($12,000), Roth IRA ($6,000), life insurance ($45,000), and savings ($8,000) all have forms, and the $9,000 car does not. Give a decimal.

ExcelPythonR


Put the amounts in B2:B6 and “Yes”/“No” for has a form in C2:C6. Find the share.






NoteSolution





=SUMIF(C2:C6, "Yes", B2:B6) / SUM(B2:B6)
This returns 0.8875, about 89% of the estate.














The bottom of the fraction is the whole estate: both piles together.


def beneficiary_share(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary):
    return sum(with_beneficiary) / (sum(with_beneficiary) + sum(without_beneficiary))

beneficiary_share([12000, 6000, 45000, 8000], [9000])















The bottom of the fraction is the whole estate: both piles together.


beneficiary_share <- function(with_beneficiary, without_beneficiary) {

title: Budgeting
text:
1 Book Topics

Mindset shift: a budget is intentional allocation, not restriction; reframe “I have to spend” as “my needs cost”; room for error is the most underrated concept (Housel)
Expense categories: fixed (lock in and automate), variable (category limits, not line by line tracking), periodic (set aside 1/12 of the annual cost each month)
Sinking funds: $1,200/year car insurance becomes $100/month; gifts $600 → $50, car maintenance $1,200 → $100, vacation $2,400 → $200
Zero-based budgeting: every dollar of a $5,000 paycheck gets a job and the remainder is $0; best for anyone rebuilding from debt or with irregular income
Percentage-based budgeting: Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan (fixed 50 to 60%, investments 10%+, savings 5 to 10%, guilt-free 20 to 35%) next to the 50/30/20 rule
Recommendation: zero-based for 2 to 3 months, then graduate to percentages with automation
Tools: a spreadsheet with tabs for income, fixed, variable, sinking funds, net worth, and a summary; the best tool is the one you will actually use
Budgeting math: percentages, annualizing and monthly-izing, opportunity cost, break-even
Financial Order of Operations: the budget shows how much is left over; Preston’s FOO shows where it goes next

2 Percentages
The foundational budgeting calculation: what share of income does each expense represent? Picture income as one bar and each expense as a slice of it.

3 Annualizing and Monthly-izing
Scale any spending habit across time periods to see the true cost. Each period is the shorter one multiplied by how many times it fits.
Formula: Cost over a longer period = Cost per period × Number of periods it contains
Daily → Weekly: × 7
Weekly → Monthly: × 4.33 (not 4)
Monthly → Annual: × 12
Daily → Annual: × 365
Annual → Monthly: ÷ 12
Book example: a $5 daily coffee is $5 × 365 = $1,825 per year.





The same $5/day habit across four time periods







The same $5/day habit across four time periods

This returns $1,825.



















How many days are in a year? How many months?


def to_annual(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": 365, "weekly": 52, "monthly": 12}
    return amount * factors[period]

to_annual(5, "daily")















How many days are in a year? How many months?


to_annual <- function(amount, period = "daily") {
  factors <- c(daily = 365, weekly = 52, monthly = 12)

}

text:
4 Opportunity Cost
Every dollar spent is also what that dollar could have become. The hidden cost of any purchase is its future value if invested instead.
Formula: amount × (1 + r)^n
Book example: choosing a $15,000 used car over a $40,000 new one and investing the $25,000 difference at 7% for 30 years gives $25,000 × (1.07)^30 ≈ $190,000.

$25,000 invested at 7%: value at each checkpoint

opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)

title: Asset Allocation
text:
1 Book Topics

Stocks, bonds, and cash: stocks grow most but can drop 30% to 50%; bonds grow slower and fall less; cash is the emergency fund and sits outside the investment split
How much in stocks when you’re young: everyone agrees on mostly stocks; Bogle (roughly your age in bonds, later 80 to 85% stocks), Sethi (80 to 90%), Collins (100% while building), Felix on the Cederburg research (100% stocks, global), Housel (extra cash for peace of mind); 80 to 90% is a reasonable start
US vs. international: 60/40 to 80/20 (US/international) is common; the Cederburg research goes to about one third US
Target date funds: one fund that sets the split and follows a glide path toward bonds; check the fee and don’t mix it with other funds
The three fund portfolio: total US stocks, total international stocks, total US bonds for about 0.05% (for example 60/30/10)
Rebalancing: check once a year and act when any part drifts more than about 5 percentage points; send new money to whatever is below target

title: Asset Allocation
text:
2 Good Years and Bad Years
A portfolio’s return is a weighted average of what each part earns.
Formula: Portfolio return = (Stock % × Stock return) + (Bond % × Bond return)
Example (stocks +10% average, −40% bad; bonds +4% average, 0% bad): an 80/20 split in a bad year is (0.80 × −40%) + (0.20 × 0%) = −32%, or −$3,200 on $10,000. In an average year it’s (0.80 × 10%) + (0.20 × 4%) = 8.8%, or +$880.





$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split







$10,000 in an average year and a bad year, by stock/bond split




The second example adds more splits and two columns compared with 100/0: the average year gain you give up and the bad year loss you avoid. The third uses the real 2008 numbers from the book (stocks about −37%, bonds about +5%), where bonds actually went up.
Read the two columns together. Going from 100/0 to 60/40 gives up $240 in an average year but cuts the bad year loss from $4,000 to $2,400. Each step toward bonds trades a little growth for a softer fall.

2.1 Level 1: Guided

=A2*B2 + (1-A2)*C2
This returns -0.32, a loss of $3,200 on $10,000.














Whatever isn’t in stocks is in bonds, and earns the bond return.


def portfolio_return(stock_pct, stock_return, bond_return):
    return stock_pct * stock_return + (1 - stock_pct) * bond_return

portfolio_return(0.80, -0.40, 0)















Whatever isn’t in stocks is in bonds, and earns the bond return.


portfolio_return <- function(stock_pct, stock_return, bond_return) {
  stock_pct * stock_return + (1 - stock_pct) * bond_return

section: 3 How Much to Move When You Rebalance
text:
3 How Much to Move When You Rebalance
When one part grows or shrinks, move just enough to get back to the target split.
Formula: Amount to move = (Target % × Total) − Current amount
Example: $10,000 at 80/20, then stocks drop 30%. Stocks are $5,600, bonds $2,000, total $7,600 (stocks about 74%). (0.80 × $7,600) − $5,600 = $480 moved from bonds into stocks.





An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing







An 80/20 portfolio before a 30% stock drop, after it, and after rebalancing




The second example runs several stock moves, up and down, and applies the book’s 5 percentage point rule to decide whether to act at all. A negative amount means sell stocks and buy bonds. The last example rebalances with new money only, so nothing gets sold.
Read a positive answer as “buy that much stock,” and a negative answer as “sell that much stock.” A 10% drop only moves the split about 2 points, so the 5 point rule says wait. With $1,000 of new money after the 30% drop, the full $1,000 goes to stocks and the gap closes from $480 to under $300 without selling anything.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish rebalance_amount(). A $10,000 80/20 portfolio has $5,600 in stocks and $2,000 in bonds after a 30% stock drop. How much should move into stocks?

=A2*(B2+C2) - B2
This returns $480: sell $480 of bonds and buy stocks.














Where you should be (target × total) minus where you are.


def rebalance_amount(target_pct, total, current_amount):
    return target_pct * total - current_amount

rebalance_amount(0.80, 5600 + 2000, 5600)















Where you should be (target × total) minus where you are.


rebalance_amount <- function(target_pct, total, current_amount) {
  target_pct * total - current_amount
}
rebalance_amount(0.80, 5600 + 2000, 5600)

The same formula returns -$480: sell $480 of stocks and buy bonds, selling high.

rebalance_amount(0.80, 10400 + 2000, 10400)


















The total is 10400 + 2000, and the current stock amount is 10400.


rebalance_amount(0.80, 10400 + 2000, 10400)









3.3 Level 3: Challenge
The book’s rule: only rebalance when stocks drift more than 5 percentage points from the 80% target. Starting from $8,000 stocks and $2,000 bonds, stocks move −30%, −10%, −5%, +10%, or +30%. In how many of those cases should you rebalance?

ExcelPythonR

NoteSolution





Stocks in B2: =8000*(1+A2). Share in C2: =B2/(B2+2000)*100. Drift in D2: =ABS(C2-80). Fill down, then =COUNTIF(D2:D6, ">5") returns 1. Only the 30% drop (73.7% stocks) crosses the band.

title: Automating Savings
text:
1 Book Topics

Why automation matters: willpower is finite; save first and spend what remains (Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan)
Money flow: split each paycheck on the first business day into savings, retirement, and checking
Method 1, direct deposit split: the cleanest approach; savings leave the paycheck before it reaches checking
Method 2, automatic bank transfers: the fallback; schedule a recurring transfer for the day after payday, never on payday itself
Pay yourself first math: Monthly Savings = Gross Monthly Income × Savings Rate, often split across an emergency fund, 401(k) match, sinking funds, and investing
Escalation: save half of every raise (Save More Tomorrow); stepping from 15% to 30% over seven years roughly doubles where you end up
Troubleshooting: lower the amount if you keep pulling money back; automate a percentage of average income if pay varies

title: Automating Savings
text:
2 Pay Yourself First
Picture your monthly income as one bar. Your savings rate is the slice carved off before you see it; the rest is what you live on.
Formula: Monthly Savings Amount = Gross Monthly Income × Savings Rate

3 Direct Deposit Split
The book’s Method 1 example: a $5,000 gross paycheck, a 25% savings goal, a 10% 401(k) contribution taken before taxes, and about $750 in taxes. The 401(k) already covers part of the goal, so the HYSA only needs the rest.
Formula: HYSA Split = (Gross × Savings Rate) − 401(k); Checking Split = Gross − 401(k) − Taxes − HYSA Split
Example: 401(k) = $500, so the HYSA split is $1,250 − $500 = $750. The deposit is $5,000 − $500 − $750 = $3,750, and checking gets $3,750 − $750 = $3,000.





Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split







Where a $5,000 gross paycheck goes with a direct deposit split




How to read this result: the HYSA and checking numbers are what you type into your payroll portal. The 401(k) and taxes are handled by payroll before the deposit.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks so deposit_split() sends the rest of the 25% goal to the HYSA after the 401(k), then find the HYSA split for a $5,000 paycheck with a 10% 401(k) and $750 of taxes.

ExcelPythonR


Put gross pay in A2 (5000), the savings rate in B2 (0.25), the 401(k) rate in C2 (0.10), and taxes in D2 (750). Find the 401(k) in E2 and the HYSA split in F2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * C2
=A2 * B2 - E2
The 401(k) takes $500 and the HYSA gets $750.














The full savings goal is gross × savings rate. The 401(k) already covers part of it.


def deposit_split(gross, savings_rate, k401_rate, taxes):
    k401 = gross * k401_rate
    hysa = gross * savings_rate - k401
    deposit = gross - k401 - taxes
    checking = deposit - hysa
    return {"k401": k401, "taxes": taxes, "deposit": deposit, "hysa": hysa, "checking": checking}

deposit_split(5000, 0.25, 0.10, 750)["hysa"]

  k401     <- gross * k401_rate
  hysa     <- gross * savings_rate - k401
  deposit  <- gross - k401 - taxes
  checking <- deposit - hysa
  data.frame(k401, taxes, deposit, hysa, checking)
}

4 Escalating with Raises
Save half of every raise. Your spending still grows a little, and your savings rate climbs without a budget cut.
Formula: Extra Monthly Savings = (New Income − Old Income) × 0.5 ÷ 12; 30 Year Value = Monthly × ((1 + r/12)^360 − 1) ÷ (r/12)
Example: a raise from $50,000 to $52,000 adds $1,000 a year ($83.33 a month) to savings. In the book’s escalation table, $625 a month at 7% for 30 years grows to about $762k, and $1,575 a month grows to about $1.92M.





30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return







30 years of saving each year’s monthly amount at a 7% return

def raise_to_savings(old_income, new_income, share=0.5):

raise_to_savings(50000, 52000)















The raise is the new income minus the old income.

title: Emergency Fund
text:
1 Book Topics

What it is: cash set aside for the unexpected so you never reach for credit; the target is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, and it is Step 4 of the Financial Order of Operations
Why it matters: most derailments start with one surprise bill charged at 20 to 24% interest; Housel frames the fund as buying options, not earning a return
Essential expenses baseline: housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health, and minimum debt payments; dining out and subscriptions do not count
Adjusting for risk: stable income with good coverage needs 3 to 4 months; dependents need 6 minimum; variable or self-employed income leans toward 6 to 9
Starter fund first: build $1,000, clear high-interest debt, then fill the full 3 to 6 month fund
Where to keep it: a high-yield savings account, money market fund, or insured credit union; not checking, stocks, long-term CDs, or cash at home
Why not the stock market: job losses and market drops tend to arrive together; Felix treats the fund as a hedge on human capital
Building it: 12 to 24 months is typical; doubling the contribution roughly halves the time; automate a payday transfer and find money in small cuts
Rebuilding: a withdrawal is the fund doing its job; resume contributions immediately without pausing retirement savings
Emergency fund math: target amount, months to reach the target, contribution needed by a deadline, and what the fund earns while you build it

title: Emergency Fund

2 Your Target Amount
Your target is your essential monthly expenses multiplied by the number of months you want to cover. Each extra month adds one more block of expenses.
Formula: Target = Monthly Essential Expenses × Months of Coverage

text:
3 Months to Reach Your Target
Given your current balance and a monthly contribution, how long until you reach the target? Part of the target bar is already filled; the monthly contributions close the gap.
Formula: Months to Goal = (Target − Current Balance) ÷ Monthly Contribution
Book example: a $14,000 target with $2,000 saved and $500/month takes (14,000 − 2,000) ÷ 500 = 24 months.





A $14,000 target with $2,000 saved: the $12,000 gap, filled $500 at a time







A $14,000 target with $2,000 saved: the $12,000 gap, filled $500 at a time





3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish months_to_ef_goal(), then find how long it takes to reach $14,000 with $2,000 saved and $500 a month.

Put the target in A2 (14000), the balance in B2 (2000), and the contribution in C2 (500). Find the whole months in D2.

=ROUNDUP(MAX(0, A2 - B2) / C2, 0)
This returns 24.














What’s left is the target minus what you already have.


import math
def months_to_ef_goal(target, current_balance, monthly_contribution):
    remaining = max(0, target - current_balance)
    return math.ceil(remaining / monthly_contribution)

months_to_ef_goal(14000, 2000, 500)















What’s left is the target minus what you already have.


months_to_ef_goal <- function(target, current_balance, monthly_contribution) {
  remaining <- max(0, target - current_balance)
  ceiling(remaining / monthly_contribution)
}

4 Contribution Needed by a Deadline
Working backwards: to reach the target by a set month, how much do you need to save each month? The number of slices is fixed, and the question is how wide each slice must be.
Formula: Monthly Contribution = (Target − Current Balance) ÷ Months Remaining

The same $12,000 gap, cut into 18 equal monthly slices







The same $12,000 gap, cut into 18 equal monthly slices

Write contribution_with_interest(target, current_balance, annual_rate, months) and find the monthly amount to reach $14,000 in 18 months from $2,000. The formula is (Target − Balance × (1 + r)^n) × r ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), with r = annual rate ÷ 12.

ExcelPythonR

NoteSolution





=PMT(4.5%/12, 18, -2000, 14000)
This returns about $638.17, about $29 a month less than ignoring interest. (Excel shows it as negative because it is money leaving your pocket.)

def contribution_with_interest(target, current_balance, annual_rate, months):
    monthly_rate = annual_rate / 12
    growth = (1 + monthly_rate) ** months
    return (target - current_balance * growth) * monthly_rate / (growth - 1)

contribution_with_interest <- function(target, current_balance, annual_rate, months) {

  growth <- (1 + monthly_rate)^months
  (target - current_balance * growth) * monthly_rate / (growth - 1)
}

text:
5 What the Fund Earns While You Build It
A fund in a high-yield savings account earns interest. It will not change your timeline much, but it is real money. Each month the balance is multiplied by (1 + the monthly rate).
Formula: Future Value = Balance × (1 + monthly rate)^months, where monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12
Book example: $14,000 at 4.5%, untouched for 12 months, grows to about $14,643.





$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest







$14,000 at 4.5% for 12 months: your balance plus interest





5.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish ef_growth(), then find what $14,000 grows to in 12 months at 4.5%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the balance in A2 (14000), the rate in B2 (0.045), and months in C2 (12). Find the balance in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2*(1+B2/12)^C2
This returns $14,643.16.














Split the yearly rate across 12 months, then compound once per month.


def ef_growth(balance, annual_rate, months):
    monthly_rate = annual_rate / 12
    return balance * (1 + monthly_rate) ** months

ef_growth(14000, 0.045, 12)















Split the yearly rate across 12 months, then compound once per month.


ef_growth <- function(balance, annual_rate, months) {
  monthly_rate <- annual_rate / 12
  balance * (1 + monthly_rate)^months
}
ef_growth(14000, 0.045, 12)

Put months 1 to 24 in A5:A28, find the interest at each month in B, then find the first month at or above $300.

title: Financial Goals
text:
1 Book Topics

Short, medium, and long goals: when you need the money decides where it lives; under 3 years in high yield savings, 3 to 10 years in savings or a bond and stock mix, over 10 years in index funds inside retirement accounts
Wish vs. goal: a goal has a number, a date, and a monthly amount; give each goal its own named savings account and automate the transfer on payday
Do you need a goal to save?: Sethi and Preston give planned expenses their own step; Housel says savings with no goal attached buys flexibility; most people do best with both
How much to save: Sethi (about 10% of take home pay for investing plus 5% to 10% for goals), The Money Guy Show (25% of gross), 15% for retirement as a starting point; start with what you can and raise it with every raise
Sequencing goals: finish the Financial Order of Operations first, then fund goals one at a time or all at once; the last goal finishes on the same day either way
Tracking progress: check transfers monthly, compare balances every few months, add up net worth once a year, and notice when you hit a goal

text:
2 Saving for a Goal with Interest
Interest does part of the work, so you can save a little less each month than goal ÷ months. This formula works backward from the future value of a monthly deposit.
Formula: Monthly amount = Goal × r ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 and n = number of months





A $15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest







A $15,000 goal in 5 years at 4%: your deposits plus interest




Example: a $15,000 down payment in 5 years at 4% takes about $226 a month, $24 less than the $250 you’d need with no interest. Over five years, interest adds about $1,425.
How to read this result: the monthly amount is your payday transfer. If it doesn’t fit your budget, push the date out before you lower the goal; an extra two years cuts the monthly amount by about 30%.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish monthly_for_goal(), then find the monthly deposit for a $15,000 down payment in 5 years at 4%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the goal in A2 (15000), the rate in B2 (0.04), and months in C2 (60). Find the monthly deposit in D2.






NoteSolution





=PMT(B2/12, C2, 0, -A2)
This returns $226.25.














Use a monthly rate, and compound once for every month.


def monthly_for_goal(goal, annual_rate, months):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    if r == 0:
        return goal / months
    return goal * r / ((1 + r) ** months - 1)

monthly_for_goal(15000, 0.04, 60)















Use a monthly rate, and compound once for every month.


monthly_for_goal <- function(goal, annual_rate, months) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  if (r == 0) return(goal / months)
  goal * r / ((1 + r)^months - 1)
}
monthly_for_goal(15000, 0.04, 60)

How much of the $15,000 comes from interest rather than your deposits?

ExcelPythonR


Find the interest in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2 - D2*C2
This returns $1,425.13.

















Your deposits are the payment times 60. Interest is the rest of the goal.

15000 - pmt * 60


















Your deposits are the payment times 60. Interest is the rest of the goal.

15000 - pmt * 60









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
Your budget allows $200 a month at most. At 4%, what is the shortest deadline in whole years (1 to 10) that keeps the deposit at or under $200?

ExcelPythonR


Put years 1 to 10 in A2:A11, the monthly deposit in B, and find the shortest deadline at or under $200.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =PMT(4%/12, A2*12, 0, -15000). Then:
=MINIFS(A2:A11, B2:B11, "<=200")
The answer is 6 years ($184.68 a month).

min(y for y in years if monthly_for_goal(15000, 0.04, y * 12) <= 200)

min(years[deposit <= 200])

3 One Goal at a Time vs. All at Once
When several goals share one monthly savings amount, the order changes when the first goal finishes. It never changes when the last one finishes.
Formula: Months to finish all goals = Total of all goals ÷ Monthly savings; Months to finish the first goal = First goal ÷ Amount going to it each month





Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly







Two goals funded with $600/month: one at a time vs. split evenly




Example: with $600 a month for a $3,000 trip and a $9,000 car, both goals are done in ($3,000 + $9,000) ÷ $600 = 20 months either way. The trip takes 5 months one at a time, or 10 months split evenly.
How to read this result: the order is a choice about which goal you want first, not about saving time overall. Put a fixed date goal (a wedding, a car on its last legs) first, or give it the bigger share.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish months_to_fund(), then find how many months a $3,000 trip takes at $600 a month.

Put the goal in A2 (3000) and the monthly amount in B2 (600). Find the whole months in C2.






NoteSolution





=ROUNDUP(A2 / B2, 0)
This returns 5.














A goal isn’t done until the last dollar is in, so always round up.


import math
def months_to_fund(goal, monthly):
    return math.ceil(goal / monthly)

months_to_fund(3000, 600)















A goal isn’t done until the last dollar is in, so always round up.


months_to_fund <- function(goal, monthly) {
  ceiling(goal / monthly)
}
months_to_fund(3000, 600)

Instead of one goal at a time, you split the $600 evenly between the trip and a $9,000 car. When is the trip funded now?

Change B2 to 300.

months_to_fund(3000, 300)

ExcelPythonR


Put the goals in A2:A4. Find the running total in B and the finishing month in C.






NoteSolution





In B2: =SUM($A$2:A2), filled down. In C2: =ROUNDUP(B2/700, 0), filled down. The months are 3, 8, and 20.

















Each goal finishes when the running total of goals so far is funded. itertools.accumulate(goals) gives the running totals.


from itertools import accumulate
goals = [2000, 3000, 9000]
[months_to_fund(total, 700) for total in accumulate(goals)]

text:
1 Book Topics

Take-home pay: your salary (gross pay) is not what lands in your account; taxes, Social Security and Medicare (7.65%), 401(k), and health plans come out first, so plan around take-home pay
Wealth vs. spending: true wealth is the income you didn’t spend, quietly compounding (Housel); conspicuous consumption is negatively correlated with actual wealth (Felix)
Human capital: early in a career, future earning potential is the biggest asset; invest in skills and career growth, and take more stock market risk when young (Felix)
Spending and happiness: experiences beat possessions; buying time is a high return use of money; lifestyle inflation is the silent killer; housing is the biggest lever
Three anchoring rules: spend on what you love, cut what you don’t (Sethi); build a gap between ego and income (Housel); keep it simple (Bogle)
Wealth formula: Wealth = Focus + (Stoicism × Time × Diversification); focus is additive, the other three multiply, so a zero on any one collapses the second term (Galloway)
As income grows: split every raise, 50% to investing and 50% to lifestyle
Math: the wealth formula as yearly savings compounding ($62,400 income, 15% saved, 8% for 40 years), the fixed-cost ratio ($1,760 of $3,200 take-home pay, under a 60% ceiling), and what a raise is really worth ($200/month at 7% for 25 years)

3 Number Formatting
Before working through the math, it helps to have two small formatting utilities that handle the $ and % symbols seen throughout the book. They take a plain number and return a reader-friendly string.

ExcelPythonR


In Excel, number formatting is applied through the toolbar. Select the cells to format and choose the appropriate option from the Number Format dropdown.







Common number formats in Excel


There are two options for money: Currency and Accounting.1


fmt_dollar() uses an f-string with , for thousands and .{digits}f for decimal places.


show/hide
def fmt_dollar(x, digits=2):
    return f"${x:,.{digits}f}"


fmt_pct() takes a decimal rate, multiplies by 100, and formats the result.


show/hide
def fmt_pct(x, digits=1):
    return f"{x * 100:.{digits}f}%"


Utility functions like fmt_pct() can be re-used in other, more complex functions.


show/hide
print(fmt_dollar(9200))
#> $9,200.00
print(fmt_dollar(4200.50))
#> $4,200.50
print(fmt_pct(0.07))
#> 7.0%
print(fmt_pct(0.456))
#> 45.6%




fmt_dollar() adds a dollar sign, comma separators, and rounds to a set number of decimal places.


show/hide
fmt_dollar <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
}


fmt_pct() expects a decimal rate (e.g. 0.07 for 7%) and converts it to a percentage string.


show/hide
fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(round(x * 100, digits), "%")
}


This can be used to format percentages as strings with a percent sign.


show/hide
fmt_dollar(9200)
#> [1] "$9,200.00"
fmt_dollar(4200.50)
#> [1] "$4,200.50"
fmt_pct(0.07)
#> [1] "7%"
fmt_pct(0.456)
#> [1] "45.6%"





Both fmt_dollar() and fmt_pct() follow the same convention: input is always a plain number, output is always a string. They are used throughout the remaining sections to clean up results.
