text:
4 The Wealth Formula
Galloway’s formula becomes real numbers when we picture someone earning $62,400 a year (about the 2025 median for full time workers). They save 15% ($9,360) every year and earn 8%. Each bar below is their savings at a checkpoint, split into what they put in and what it grew into.
Formula: Wealth after n years = Yearly savings × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Yearly savings = Income × Savings rate, r is the yearly return, and n is the number of years.





$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth







$9,360 saved every year at 8%: money put in vs. growth




The blue layer grows in a straight line, one $9,360 deposit per year. The green layer is growth, and it passes the blue layer after about year 18.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish wealth_formula(), then find the wealth after 40 years: $62,400 income, 15% saved, 8% return.

ExcelPythonR


Put the inputs in A2 (62400), B2 (0.15), C2 (0.08), and D2 (40). In E2, write a formula for total wealth (money put in plus growth).






NoteSolution





=(A2*B2)*(((1+C2)^D2-1)/C2)
Or use =FV(C2, D2, -A2*B2). Both return $2,424,769.














Yearly savings is income times the savings rate. The growth factor uses the yearly return.


def wealth_formula(median_income, savings_rate, annual_return, years):
    annual_savings = median_income * savings_rate
    return annual_savings * (((1 + annual_return) ** years - 1) / annual_return)

wealth_formula(62400, 0.15, 0.08, 40)















Yearly savings is income times the savings rate. The growth factor uses the yearly return.


wealth_formula <- function(median_income, savings_rate, annual_return, years) {
  annual_savings <- median_income * savings_rate
  annual_savings * (((1 + annual_return)^years - 1) / annual_return)
}
wealth_formula(62400, 0.15, 0.08, 40)

Growth is $1,039,374 of the $1,413,774 total.

put_in = 62400 * 0.20 * 30
total - put_in

5 Fixed-Cost Ratio
Fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, utilities) are the bills you can’t easily change month to month. Picture a first job with $3,200 of take-home pay a month and $1,760 of fixed costs. The bar below cuts that paycheck into 10 equal pieces of $320 (each piece is 10%).
Formula: Fixed-Cost Ratio = Fixed Costs ÷ Take-Home Pay × 100





$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending







$3,200 take-home pay in 10 units of $320: fixed costs vs. flexible spending




The red section covers 5 and a half of the 10 pieces, so fixed costs take 55% of the paycheck. The ceiling is 60% of $3,200, or $1,920.

6 Using Pipes in R
The pipe operator (|>) passes the output of one function directly into the next function as its first argument, so the code reads left to right instead of inside out. fixed_cost_ratio() already multiplies by 100, so we can pipe its result into round() and then paste0() to add the percent sign.
fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200) |> round(1) |> paste0("%")
Read that as: compute the ratio, then round it, then add the %. The version without a pipe nests the calls and reads from the inside out, which is harder to follow.
paste0(round(fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200), 1), "%")
When steps always belong together, wrap them in a single function so callers only see one name.

fixed_cost_pct <- function(fixed_costs, take_home) {
  fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home) |>
    round(1) |>
    paste0("%")
}


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs = 1760, take_home = 3200)
#> [1] "55%"

Python has no native pipe operator. The equivalent is storing the result from fixed_cost_ratio() in a variable and passing it to the next step:

def fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs, take_home):
    ratio = fixed_cost_ratio(fixed_costs, take_home)
    return f"{ratio:.1f}%"


fixed_cost_pct(fixed_costs=1760, take_home=3200)
#> '55.0%'

Python’s approach emphasizes explicit intermediate steps. This reads top to bottom and makes debugging easier since you can inspect ratio along the way.
Read more about the pipe operator in R vs. Python.

Each step after the pipe takes the previous result as its first argument: round(1), then paste0("%").

7 What a Raise Is Really Worth
Say a raise adds $400 a month to your take-home pay, and you split it: $200 goes to your lifestyle and $200 gets invested. The chart shows what that single habit produces at 7% over 25 years.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
PMT is the amount invested each month, r is the monthly return (7% ÷ 12), and n is the number of months (25 × 12 = 300).





$200/month invested at 7%: value at each 5-year checkpoint







$200/month invested at 7%: value at each 5-year checkpoint





7.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish raise_invested_value(), then find the value of investing half of a $400 raise for 25 years at 7%.

ExcelPythonR


Use the built in FV(rate, nper, pmt) function with a monthly rate, a number of months, and the monthly contribution as a negative number.






NoteSolution





=FV(7%/12, 25*12, -200)
This returns $162,014.34.














The contribution is the share of the raise you invest. The yearly rate is split across 12 months.


def raise_invested_value(monthly_raise, invest_share, rate, years):
    contribution = monthly_raise * invest_share
    monthly_rate = rate / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return contribution * (((1 + monthly_rate) ** periods - 1) / monthly_rate)

raise_invested_value(400, 0.5, 0.07, 25)















The contribution is the share of the raise you invest. The yearly rate is split across 12 months.


raise_invested_value <- function(monthly_raise, invest_share, rate, years) {
  contribution <- monthly_raise * invest_share
  monthly_rate <- rate / 12
  periods      <- years * 12
  contribution * (((1 + monthly_rate)^periods - 1) / monthly_rate)
}
raise_invested_value(400, 0.5, 0.07, 25)

Growth is $153,022 of the $243,022 total.

put_in = 400 * 0.75 * 25 * 12
value - put_in

title: Index Funds
text:
1 Book Topics

What an index fund is: an index is a list of companies (like the S&P 500); an index fund buys everything on the list, weighted by company size (market cap), with no manager picking winners (passive vs. active)
Why index funds win: SPIVA shows 79% of large US active funds trailed the S&P 500 in 2025 and about 9 in 10 over 15 years; Bogle’s math says the average investor earns the market return minus costs
Expense ratios: a yearly fee taken out quietly; 0.04% vs. 1% is $4 vs. $100 on $10,000; look for funds under 0.10%
Total market vs. S&P 500 vs. international: the first two move almost together; experts disagree on how much international to hold (Bogle and Collins little or none, Felix anywhere from 10% to 60% home country)
ETFs vs. mutual funds: same holdings, different packaging; ETFs trade all day and are a little more tax efficient, mutual funds make automatic investing easier
How to pick one: go broad, check the expense ratio, look for “index” in the 401(k) list (or a target date fund), automate, and leave it alone

title: Index Funds
text:
2 The Fee This Year
Every year, the fund takes a slice of your balance as its fee.
Formula: Yearly fee = Balance × Expense ratio
Example: $10,000 × 0.0004 = $4. $10,000 × 0.01 = $100, or 25 times as much.





One year of fees on $10,000







One year of fees on $10,000




The second example uses a table of typical expense ratios across a few balances. The fee grows with your balance, so a fee that costs pocket change at $10,000 costs real money at $250,000.
Read the fee as dollars you never see. The active fund costs $2,500 a year on $250,000, and the index fund costs $100.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish yearly_fee(), then find this year’s fee on $10,000 in an index fund with a 0.04% expense ratio.

Put the balance in A2 (10000) and the expense ratio in B2 (0.0004). Find the fee in C2.

=A2 * B2
This returns $4.

def yearly_fee(balance, expense_ratio):
    return balance * expense_ratio

yearly_fee(10000, 0.0004)















The fee is a percentage of your balance. 0.04% is 0.0004.


yearly_fee <- function(balance, expense_ratio) {
  balance * expense_ratio
}
yearly_fee(10000, 0.0004)

An active fund charges 1%. What is this year’s fee on a $250,000 balance?

ExcelPythonR


Change A2 to 250000 and B2 to 0.01.






NoteSolution





The same formula returns $2,500, every year, whether the fund does well or not.

















Write 1% as 0.01.


yearly_fee(250000, 0.01)


















Write 1% as 0.01.

section: 3 What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
text:
3 What Fees Cost Over a Lifetime
The fee comes out of the return, so subtract it from the return before you compound.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r], where r = (return − expense ratio) ÷ 12
Example: $300/month for 40 years at 7%. The index fund (0.04%) grows to about $778,655 and the active fund (1%) to about $597,447. Both people put in the same $144,000. The 1% fee cost $181,207, about 23% of what the index fund investor ended up with.





$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee







$300/month at 7%, with a 0.04% fee vs. a 1% fee




The second example tries several expense ratios over 40 years and reports the share of the low cost result each one loses. The edge case is a 0% fee, which is just the plain annuity from Investing Basics.
Read the lifetime cost as a share, not a dollar amount. A 1% fee takes about 23% of the ending balance, which is why the book says close to a quarter. A negative “lost” number means that fund beat the 0.04% index fund (only possible here with a lower fee).

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish future_value_after_fees(), then find what $300 a month grows to over 40 years at 7% in an index fund charging 0.04%.

ExcelPythonR


Find the value in one formula with the fee taken off the return.






NoteSolution





=FV((7%-0.04%)/12, 480, -300)
This returns $778,654.71.














The fee comes straight off the return. 0.04% is 0.0004.


def future_value_after_fees(contribution, annual_return, expense_ratio, years):
    rate = (annual_return - expense_ratio) / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return contribution * (((1 + rate) ** periods - 1) / rate)

future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.0004, 40)















The fee comes straight off the return. 0.04% is 0.0004.


future_value_after_fees <- function(contribution, annual_return, expense_ratio, years) {
  rate    <- (annual_return - expense_ratio) / 12
  periods <- years * 12
  contribution * (((1 + rate)^periods - 1) / rate)
}
future_value_after_fees(300, 0.07, 0.0004, 40)

title: Investing Basics
text:
1 Book Topics

Compounding: interest earning interest; the Rule of 72 says years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return % (about 10 years at 7%, about 7 years at 10%); $10,000 at 7% for 40 years
The core portfolio: stocks (70 to 90% with 20+ years), bonds (10 to 30%), and cash (the emergency fund, kept separate); a simple default is 80% total stock market and 20% total bond market index funds, rebalanced once a year for about 0.03% in fees
Risk vs. return: 100% stocks might average 10% but drop 40% in a bad year; 60/40 averages about 7% and drops about 20%; pick the split you can stick with through a bear market
Diversification: one dollar in a total market fund owns thousands of companies, so one failure barely matters
Tax-advantaged accounts: 2026 limits for the 401(k)/403(b) ($24,500), Roth and Traditional IRA ($7,500), HSA ($4,400 self), and taxable accounts; fill them in order (401(k) to the match, Roth IRA or HSA, max the 401(k), then taxable); $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to about $76,000, saving about $13,200 in taxes in a Roth
Common mistakes: timing the market, chasing past performance, paying high fees (1% over 30 years costs about 25%), holding too much cash, and selling in a panic

title: Investing Basics
section: 2 Future Value and the Rule of 72
text:
2 Future Value and the Rule of 72
Each year’s growth is applied to a bigger base, so the balance curves upward instead of rising in a straight line.
Formula: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n
Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return %
Example: $10,000 at 7% for 10 years grows to about $19,672, and at 7% money doubles roughly every 10 years.





$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint







$10,000 growing at 7%: value at each checkpoint




The Rule of 72 is a shortcut. The exact doubling time is log(2) ÷ log(1 + r). The shortcut is very close for returns between about 4% and 12%, and drifts further off at the extremes.
Read the result as “what one deposit becomes if you leave it alone.” At 7%, the Rule of 72 says 10.3 years and the exact answer is 10.2 years, so the shortcut is good enough for planning.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish future_value(), then find what $10,000 grows to in 10 years at 7%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the amount in A2 (10000), the rate in B2 (0.07), and years in C2 (10). Find the future value in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2*(1+B2)^C2
This returns $19,671.51. =FV(B2, C2, 0, -A2) gives the same answer.














Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.


def future_value(present_value, rate, years):
    return present_value * (1 + rate) ** years

future_value(10000, 0.07, 10)















Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.


future_value <- function(present_value, rate, years) {
  present_value * (1 + rate)^years
}
future_value(10000, 0.07, 10)

future_value(10000, 0.07, 40)









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
The Rule of 72 (72 ÷ return %) estimates doubling time. The exact time is ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + r). For whole-number returns from 1% to 15%, at which return is the rule closest to exact?

ExcelPythonR


Put returns 1 to 15 in A2:A16. Find the rule in B, the exact time in C, and the gap in D, then the return with the smallest gap.






NoteSolution





In B2: =72/A2. In C2: =LN(2)/LN(1+A2/100). In D2: =ABS(B2-C2). Fill down, then:
=INDEX(A2:A16, MATCH(MIN(D2:D16), D2:D16, 0))
The answer is 8%: 9 years by the rule, 9.006 exact.














The exact time is math.log(2) / math.log(1 + r / 100). Use min(returns, key=lambda r: abs(...)).

returns = range(1, 16)
min(returns, key=lambda r: abs(72 / r - math.log(2) / math.log(1 + r / 100)))

gap <- abs(72 / returns - log(2) / log(1 + returns / 100))
returns[which.min(gap)]

title: Investing Basics
text:
3 Future Value of Regular Contributions
Investing a fixed amount every month builds wealth two ways: the money you put in, and the growth on everything you put in before.
Formula: FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r]
Example: $500/month for 30 years (360 months) at a 7% annual return (about 0.583% per month) grows to about $610,000, and only $180,000 of that is money you put in.





$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains







$500/month contributions at 7%: contributed vs. gains




Starting earlier matters more than putting in more. The second example compares the same $500/month started at 25, 35, and 45, all ending at 65. The book’s recap number ($50/month for 30 years is about $61,000) is the same math at one tenth the size.
Read the result as two layers. At 30 years, about 70% of the $610,000 is growth, not deposits. Starting at 25 instead of 45 more than quadruples the ending balance while only doubling what you put in.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish future_value_series(), then find what $500 a month grows to in 30 years at a 7% yearly return.

ExcelPythonR


Find the value in one formula with a monthly rate and 360 months.






NoteSolution





=FV(7%/12, 360, -500)
This returns $609,985.50.














The growth factor is raised to the number of periods, and divided by the rate.


def future_value_series(contribution, rate, periods):
    return contribution * (((1 + rate) ** periods - 1) / rate)

future_value_series(500, 0.07 / 12, 30 * 12)















The growth factor is raised to the number of periods, and divided by the rate.


future_value_series <- function(contribution, rate, periods) {
  contribution * (((1 + rate)^periods - 1) / rate)

text:
4 Real (Inflation-Adjusted) Return
Inflation shrinks what each dollar buys, so the return that matters is what’s left after inflation.
Formula: Real Return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1
Example: (1.07 ÷ 1.03) − 1 = about 3.88%, a little less than the 4% you’d get by simple subtraction.





Nominal return, inflation, and real return







Nominal return, inflation, and real return




The second example compares several investments against 3% inflation. Cash earning 4% (one of the book’s common mistakes) barely beats inflation, and cash earning less than inflation has a negative real return. The last line shows what $76,123 (the book’s 30 year example) is worth in today’s dollars.
Read a negative real return as “losing buying power, even though the balance went up.” The $76,123 in 30 years buys about what $31,400 buys today, which is why the book says to think in real terms.

Fill in the blanks to finish real_return(), then find the real return of 7% against 3% inflation. Give a decimal.

This returns 0.0388, a little under the 4% from simple subtraction.














Divide what your money grows by (1 + nominal) by what prices grow by (1 + inflation).


def real_return(nominal, inflation):
    return (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1

real_return(0.07, 0.03)

  (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1

title: Managing Debt
text:
1 Book Topics

Debt hierarchy: every debt has a price (its APR); toxic debt (15 to 29% APR: credit cards, payday loans) gets attacked first, moderate debt (5 to 10%: car loans, private student loans) gets paid down steadily, and strategic debt (3 to 7%: mortgages, federal student loans) gets paid on schedule
Credit cards: pay them off before nearly every other goal (except insurance deductibles and an employer match); the playbook is stop using them, negotiate the APR, pick avalanche or snowball, consider a 0% transfer or cheaper loan, and automate minimums; once paid in full monthly, use cards as a payment tool
Student loans: the return depends on the income premium the degree creates; the 1× rule caps total debt at your expected first year salary, which works out to roughly 14% of gross pay on a standard 10 year plan at 6.5%
Federal IDR plans: payments are a share of discretionary income (AGI minus a multiple of the poverty guideline); SAVE ended in March 2026, RAP starts July 2026 (1 to 10% of AGI, 30 years), IBR is the stable fallback, and PSLF forgives the rest after 10 years of public service
Pay off vs. invest: compare the loan rate to your expected after tax return (above 6% pay off, 4 to 6% do both, below 4% invest), then add a peace of mind premium
Car loans: depreciating assets financed at 7 to 9%; buy used, pay cash, keep loans under 36 months, follow the 20/4/10 rule
Debt and the FOO: high interest debt is step 3, low interest debt is step 9; moderate debt sits in between, after emergency reserves

title: Managing Debt
text:
2 APR vs. APY
Lenders quote the APR. You actually pay the APY, which is higher because interest compounds.
Formula: APY = (1 + APR ÷ n)^n − 1, where n is the number of compounding periods per year
Example: a 24% APR compounded daily is about 27.1% APY. On a $10,000 balance that is an extra $310 a year.





APR cost vs. APY cost on a $10,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)







APR cost vs. APY cost on a $10,000 balance (24% APR, daily compounding)




The gap grows as the APR grows. It also grows with how often interest compounds, but most of the jump happens going from yearly to monthly. Daily adds only a little more. If APR and APY are the same, interest compounds once a year.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish apr_to_apy(), then find the APY of a 24% APR card that compounds daily. Give the answer as a decimal.

ExcelPythonR


Put the APR in A2 (0.24) and the compounding periods in B2 (365). Find the APY in C2.






NoteSolution





=(1 + A2/B2)^B2 - 1
This returns 0.2711, or 27.1%. Excel’s =EFFECT(A2, B2) gives the same answer.














The APR is split across every compounding period, and it compounds that many times a year.


def apr_to_apy(apr, periods_per_year=365):
    return (1 + apr / periods_per_year) ** periods_per_year - 1

apr_to_apy(0.24)















The APR is split across every compounding period, and it compounds that many times a year.


apr_to_apy <- function(apr, periods_per_year = 365) {
  (1 + apr / periods_per_year)^periods_per_year - 1
}
apr_to_apy(0.24)

title: Managing Debt
text:
3 Minimum Payments
Minimum payments barely touch the balance. Most of each payment goes to interest. As the balance falls, a little more of each payment goes to principal, and the formula accounts for that.
Formula: Months to pay off = −ln(1 − r × Balance ÷ Payment) ÷ ln(1 + r), where r = APR ÷ 12
Example: $5,000 at 22% APR, paying $100 a month. The first month’s interest is about $92, so only $8 reduces the balance. Payoff takes about 137 months (11 years), and you pay about $13,700 in total.





Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes







Where a $100 minimum payment actually goes




The formula only works when the payment is bigger than the first month’s interest. If it isn’t, the balance never shrinks, and the answer comes back as NaN (not a number). Small increases in the payment cut years off the debt.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish months_to_payoff(), then find how many months it takes to clear $5,000 at 22% APR paying $100 a month.

ExcelPythonR


Put the balance in A2 (5000), the payment in B2 (100), and the APR in C2 (0.22). Find the months in D2.






NoteSolution





=NPER(C2/12, -B2, A2)
This returns about 136.8 months, or 11 years.














The monthly rate is the APR divided by 12. The formula uses the balance in the second blank.


import math
def months_to_payoff(balance, monthly_payment, apr):
    r = apr / 12
    return -math.log(1 - r * balance / monthly_payment) / math.log(1 + r)

months_to_payoff(5000, 100, 0.22)















The monthly rate is the APR divided by 12. The formula uses the balance in the second blank.


months_to_payoff <- function(balance, monthly_payment, apr) {
  r <- apr / 12
  -log(1 - r * balance / monthly_payment) / log(1 + r)
}
months_to_payoff(5000, 100, 0.22)

months * 200 - 5000

months * 200 - 5000

You want the $5,000 card (22% APR) gone in 3 years. Write payment_needed(balance, apr, years) using the loan payment formula, Payment = Balance × r(1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1) with r = APR ÷ 12 and n = months, and find the monthly payment.

section: 4 Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
text:
4 Total Interest Over a Loan’s Life
For any installment loan (car, mortgage, student loan), the real cost is everything you pay minus what you borrowed.
Formula: Total Interest = (Monthly Payment × Number of Payments) − Loan Principal
Example: a $30,000 car loan at 7%. Over 6 years ($512 a month) you pay $6,864 in interest. Over 4 years ($719 a month) you pay $4,512. The shorter term saves $2,352.





$30,000 car loan: principal vs. interest for 6-year and 4-year terms







$30,000 car loan: principal vs. interest for 6-year and 4-year terms




The book rounds the payments to whole dollars. The exact payments are $511.47 and $718.39, so the exact interest is a few dollars lower. Each extra year on the loan adds interest, but the monthly payment drops less than you might expect.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish total_interest(), then find the interest on a $30,000 car loan paid at $512 a month for 6 years.

ExcelPythonR


Put the payment in A2 (512), the months in B2 (72), and the principal in C2 (30000). Find the interest in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2*B2 - C2
This returns $6,864.














Everything you pay, minus the amount you borrowed.


def total_interest(monthly_payment, n_months, principal):
    return (monthly_payment * n_months) - principal

total_interest(512, 72, 30000)















Everything you pay, minus the amount you borrowed.


total_interest <- function(monthly_payment, n_months, principal) {
  (monthly_payment * n_months) - principal
}
total_interest(512, 72, 30000)









4.2 Level 2: Practice
The same loan over 4 years costs $719 a month. How much interest does the shorter loan save compared with the 6-year loan?

ExcelPythonR


Add the 4-year loan in row 3 and find the savings.






NoteSolution





=D2 - D3
The 4-year loan’s interest is $4,512, so it saves $2,352.

5 Student Loan to Income & Standard Payment
The 1× rule says your student loans should not be bigger than your expected first year salary. Two numbers check it: the loan to income ratio, and the monthly payment that loan creates on a standard 10 year plan.
Formula: Loan to income ratio = Total loans ÷ Expected salary, and Monthly payment = Loan × r(1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where r = yearly rate ÷ 12 and n = 120 payments
Example: $45,000 ÷ $42,000 = about 1.07×, and the standard payment at 6.5% is about $511 a month.





$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary







$45,000 in student loans vs. a $42,000 starting salary




A ratio above 1.0 means the loan bar runs past the salary line. At exactly 1×, every dollar borrowed costs about $0.0114 a month, so the payment is about 14% of gross pay no matter the major. What changes is how many dollars are left over.

6 Income Driven Repayment Monthly Payment
Federal IDR plans protect part of your income and charge a percentage of the rest (your discretionary income).
Formula: Monthly payment = (AGI − threshold × Federal Poverty Guideline) × payment rate ÷ 12
Example (IBR): ($50,000 − 1.5 × $15,650) × 10% ÷ 12 = about $221 a month. For IBR loans from before July 2014 (15% rate), it is about $332.





$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment







$50,000 AGI under IBR: protected income, discretionary income, and the yearly payment




If your AGI is below the protected amount, the payment is $0. Each extra $1,000 of income above that line adds only about $8 a month under IBR. SAVE used the same formula with a 225% threshold and a 5% undergraduate rate, but it ended in March 2026. RAP uses a sliding share of total AGI instead, so this function does not cover it.

6.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish idr_monthly_payment() for IBR, then find the payment on a $50,000 AGI. Discretionary income is AGI minus 1.5 × the $15,650 poverty guideline.

ExcelPythonR


Put the AGI in A2 (50000). Find the monthly IBR payment in B2.






NoteSolution





=ROUND(MAX(0, A2 - 1.5*15650) * 10% / 12, 2)
This returns $221.04.














Use the threshold to scale the poverty guideline, then apply the payment rate.


def idr_monthly_payment(agi, poverty_guideline=15650, threshold_pct=1.5, payment_rate=0.10):
    discretionary = max(0, agi - poverty_guideline * threshold_pct)
    return round((discretionary * payment_rate) / 12, 2)

idr_monthly_payment(50000)















Use the threshold to scale the poverty guideline, then apply the payment rate.


idr_monthly_payment <- function(agi, poverty_guideline = 15650,
                                threshold_pct = 1.5, payment_rate = 0.10) {
  discretionary <- max(0, agi - poverty_guideline * threshold_pct)
  round((discretionary * payment_rate) / 12, 2)
}
idr_monthly_payment(50000)

text:
7 Debt to Income Ratio (DTI)
Lenders calculate this about you. Calculate it yourself first.
Formula: DTI = (Total Monthly Debt Payments ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Example: $2,500 in debt payments on $7,000 gross income is about 36% DTI.
Benchmarks: below 20% healthy; 20 to 35% manageable; 36 to 43% stretched; above 43% danger zone (most mortgage lenders say no).





$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income







$7,000 monthly income split into debt payments and remaining income




DTI uses gross pay (before taxes), so it looks smaller than how it feels. At about 36%, this borrower sits right on the line between manageable and stretched. Paying off one $400 car payment would bring them to about 30%.

NoteSolution

This returns 35.7.

def dti_ratio(monthly_debt_payments, gross_monthly_income):

dti_ratio(2500, 7000)

text:
8 Pay Off vs. Invest Comparison
Should extra money go to the loan or to investments? Compare the two rates.
Formula: Yearly edge of investing = Expected after tax investment return − After tax loan interest rate
A positive answer favors investing. A negative answer favors paying off the debt.
Example: a 5% mortgage vs. an expected 7% return. 7% − 5% = 2%, so the math favors investing by about 2% a year. But the 5% is guaranteed and the 7% is not.





Guaranteed 5% debt payoff vs. expected 7% investment return







Guaranteed 5% debt payoff vs. expected 7% investment return




A 2% edge sounds small, but it compounds. On $10,000 over 10 years, it is the gap between about $16,300 (the guaranteed path) and about $19,700 (the expected path). The book’s rule of thumb also adds a middle zone: between 4% and 6%, do both.

8.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish payoff_vs_invest(), then compare a 5% mortgage with an expected 7% return.

ExcelPythonR


Put the loan rate in A2 (0.05) and the expected return in B2 (0.07). Write the decision in C2.






NoteSolution





=IF(A2 > B2, "Pay off the debt", IF(A2 < B2, "Invest the difference", "Roughly a wash; do both"))














If the loan costs more than investing earns, pay it off. Otherwise invest. Use the labels “Pay off the debt” and “Invest the difference”.


def payoff_vs_invest(loan_rate, expected_return):
    if loan_rate > expected_return:
        return "Pay off the debt"
    elif loan_rate < expected_return:
        return "Invest the difference"
    return "Roughly a wash; do both"

payoff_vs_invest(0.05, 0.07)















If the loan costs more than investing earns, pay it off. Otherwise invest. Use the labels “Pay off the debt” and “Invest the difference”.


payoff_vs_invest <- function(loan_rate, expected_return) {
  if (loan_rate > expected_return) {
    "Pay off the debt"
  } else if (loan_rate < expected_return) {
    "Invest the difference"
  } else {
    "Roughly a wash; do both"
  }
}
payoff_vs_invest(0.05, 0.07)

Put a number on that 2% edge. You have $10,000. After 10 years, how much more do you have by investing at 7% than by paying down the 5% mortgage (which “earns” 5%)?

This returns $3,382.57.

The book’s rule of thumb: above 6% pay it off, 4% to 6% do both, below 4% invest. Write book_rule(loan_rate) that returns “Pay off”, “Do both”, or “Invest”, and apply it to loans at 3%, 5%, and 7%.

NoteSolution

    elif loan_rate >= 0.04:
        return "Do both"

[book_rule(r) for r in [0.03, 0.05, 0.07]]

title: Managing Debt
text:
9 Avalanche vs. Snowball Math
Two ways to order several debts. Avalanche pays the highest APR first and saves the most. Snowball pays the smallest balance first and builds momentum.
Formula: Monthly interest saved by an extra payment = Extra payment × APR ÷ 12
Example: an extra $100 on Card B (24%) saves $2.00 of interest next month. The same $100 on Card A (18%) saves $1.50.





Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)







Avalanche order (highest APR first) vs. snowball order (smallest balance first)




The book says to find the cost of snowball with a payoff calculator. The extra code below is a small one. It pays every minimum, sends the rest of a fixed monthly budget to the target debt, and rolls each freed up payment onto the next debt. The difference in total interest is the price of the snowball’s quick early wins. With these three cards, snowball costs about $338 more and takes one extra month.

NoteSolution





=INDEX(A2:A4, MATCH(MAX(C2:C4), C2:C4, 0))
This returns Card B (24%).

  pull(name)

NoteSolution





=INDEX(A2:A4, MATCH(MIN(B2:B4), B2:B4, 0))
This returns Card A ($1,000).

debts.sort_values("balance").iloc[0]["name"]


















arrange(balance) sorts smallest first. Then slice(1) and pull(name).

  arrange(balance) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(name)

payoff_sim() pays the minimums ($25, $100, $40) and sends the rest of a $400 monthly budget to the first card in order. It returns the months and total interest. How much more interest does the snowball cost than the avalanche?

NoteSolution





The avalanche pays $1,782.34 of interest over 25 months and the snowball $2,120.62 over 26, so the snowball costs $338.28 more.

text:
10 Credit Utilization Ratio
How much of your available credit you are using. High use signals stress to credit scoring models.
Formula: Utilization = (Current Balance ÷ Credit Limit) × 100
Keep it under 30% on each card and across all cards. Under 10% is ideal.
Example: a $3,000 balance on a $10,000 limit is 30% utilization, right at the threshold.





$3,000 balance against a $10,000 credit limit: used vs. unused







$3,000 balance against a $10,000 credit limit: used vs. unused

credit_utilization(3000, 10000)

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
1 Book Topics

What a retirement account is: a container, not an investment; it decides how the investments inside get taxed; early withdrawals before 59 and a half usually cost a 10% penalty plus income tax
2026 limits: 401(k)/403(b)/TSP $24,500; Traditional and Roth IRA $7,500 (one shared limit); HSA $4,400 (self); taxable brokerage has no limit
The plan at work: contributions come out of each paycheck; a common match is “50% of the first 6%”; watch vesting and don’t settle for the automatic enrollment rate
Traditional vs. Roth: pay tax later or pay it now; the only thing that matters is whether your tax rate is lower now or later, so Roth is the usual default early in a career
The IRA: opened at a brokerage, yours no matter where you work; Roth contributions (not earnings) can come out any time; Roth income limit is $153,000 to $168,000 (single)
The HSA: needs an HSA eligible (high deductible) plan; tax free going in, growing, and coming out for medical costs
Which account first: deductible cash, full match, high interest debt, emergency fund, HSA and Roth IRA, more 401(k), then taxable; aim for 15% of income including the match
Changing jobs: roll the old plan over directly; cashing out $5,000 at 22 leaves about $3,900 instead of about $100,000 by 67

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
2 The Employer Match
Your employer adds money on top of what you put in, up to a limit.
Formula: Match = Salary × min(Your %, Match limit %) × Match rate
Example: $45,000 × min(6%, 6%) × 50% = $1,350 a year in free money. At 3%, you’d only get $675.





6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match







6% of a $45,000 salary, plus a 50% employer match




The second example runs the same job across several contribution rates. Past 6%, your own deposits keep growing but the match stops. The last example shows what one year of the full match becomes if it stays invested for 40 years at 7%.
Read the match as a 50% return the day you deposit. Contributing 3% instead of 6% leaves $675 a year on the table, and one year of the full match grows to about $20,200 over 40 years at 7%.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish employer_match(), then find the yearly match on a $45,000 salary when you contribute 6% and the employer matches 50% of the first 6%.

ExcelPythonR


Put the salary in A2 (45000), your contribution in B2 (0.06), the match limit in C2 (0.06), and the match rate in D2 (0.5). Find the match in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * MIN(B2, C2) * D2
This returns $1,350.














The employer only matches up to the limit, so use the smaller of your % and the limit.


def employer_match(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate):
    return salary * min(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate

employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)















The employer only matches up to the limit, so use the smaller of your % and the limit. pmin() does it element by element.


employer_match <- function(salary, contribution_pct, match_limit_pct, match_rate) {
  salary * pmin(contribution_pct, match_limit_pct) * match_rate
}
employer_match(45000, 0.06, 0.06, 0.50)

Same job, but you only contribute 3%. What is the match now?

ExcelPythonR


Change B2 to 0.03.






NoteSolution





The same formula returns $675. Half the match is left on the table.

















Only your contribution changes: 0.03.


employer_match(45000, 0.03, 0.06, 0.50)


















Only your contribution changes: 0.03.


employer_match(45000, 0.03, 0.06, 0.50)

Five coworkers each earn $45,000 with the same 50%-of-6% match, contributing 0%, 3%, 6%, 10%, and 15%. The full match is $1,350. How much match do they miss in total?

ExcelPythonR


Put the rates in A2:A6, the match in B, and the missed match in C, then total it.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =45000*MIN(A2, 6%)*50%. In C2: =1350 - B2. Then =SUM(C2:C6) returns $2,025. Contributing more than 6% doesn’t earn more match.

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
3 Traditional vs. Roth
Roth takes the tax out first, then the rest grows. Traditional lets the whole amount grow, then takes the tax out at the end.
Formula: Amount you keep = Contribution × (1 − tax rate) × (1 + r)^n
For Roth, use today’s tax rate. For Traditional, use your tax rate in retirement.
Example: $1,000 for 40 years at 7%. With 12% now and 12% later, both accounts leave you about $13,178. If your rate in retirement is 22% instead, the Traditional account leaves you about $11,680.





$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later







$1,000 after 40 years at 7%, with a 12% tax rate now and later




Multiplying by (1 − tax rate) gives the same answer whether you do it first or last. So the second example holds today’s rate at 12% and tries several retirement rates. The edge case is a retirement rate lower than today’s, where Traditional wins.
Read the result as a contest between two tax rates. Growth and years don’t pick the winner. Roth wins when today’s rate is lower than your rate in retirement, and Traditional wins when it’s higher.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish after_tax_value(), then find what $1,000 in a Roth leaves you after 40 years at 7%, taxed at today’s 12% rate.

ExcelPythonR


Put the contribution in A2 (1000), the tax rate in B2 (0.12), the return in C2 (0.07), and years in D2 (40). Find the after-tax value in E2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * (1 - B2) * (1 + C2)^D2
This returns $13,177.52.














Taxes take a share of the money; growth multiplies it once per year.


def after_tax_value(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years):
    return contribution * (1 - tax_rate) * (1 + rate) ** years

after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)















Taxes take a share of the money; growth multiplies it once per year.


after_tax_value <- function(contribution, tax_rate, rate, years) {
  contribution * (1 - tax_rate) * (1 + rate)^years
}
after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)









3.2 Level 2: Practice
In a Traditional account, the same $1,000 is taxed when you take it out. If your retirement tax rate is 22%, what do you keep?

ExcelPythonR


Change B2 to 0.22.






NoteSolution





The same formula returns $11,680.08, about $1,500 less than the Roth.

















Only the tax rate changes: 0.22.


after_tax_value(1000, 0.22, 0.07, 40)


















Only the tax rate changes: 0.22.


after_tax_value(1000, 0.22, 0.07, 40)









3.3 Level 3: Challenge
Today’s rate is 12% (the Roth). Compare it with a Traditional account at retirement rates of 10%, 12%, 22%, and 24%. Label each “Roth”, “Traditional”, or “tie” (within $1).

ExcelPythonR


Put the retirement rates in A2:A5. Find the Traditional value in B, then the winner in C against the Roth’s $13,177.52.






NoteSolution





In B2, filled down: =1000*(1-A2)*1.07^40. In C2, filled down:
=IF(ABS(13177.52-B2)<1, "tie", IF(13177.52>B2, "Roth", "Traditional"))
The winners are Traditional, tie, Roth, Roth.

















Write a small function that compares roth with after_tax_value(1000, r, 0.07, 40), checking the tie first, and use a list comprehension.


roth = after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)
later = [0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24]
def winner(r):
    trad = after_tax_value(1000, r, 0.07, 40)
    if abs(roth - trad) < 1:
        return "tie"
    return "Roth" if roth > trad else "Traditional"

[winner(r) for r in later]


















trad <- after_tax_value(1000, later, 0.07, 40) works on all four rates. Then case_when() with the tie test first.


roth <- after_tax_value(1000, 0.12, 0.07, 40)
later <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24)
trad <- after_tax_value(1000, later, 0.07, 40)
case_when(
  abs(roth - trad) < 1 ~ "tie",
  roth > trad ~ "Roth",
  .default = "Traditional"
)

title: Retirement Accounts
text:
4 Cashing Out vs. Rolling Over
The book’s job change example: cash out $5,000 at 22, or leave it invested until 67.
Formula: Cash in hand = Balance × (1 − tax rate − penalty); Left invested = Balance × (1 + r)^n
Example: $5,000 × (1 − 0.12 − 0.10) = $3,900 today, vs. $5,000 × 1.07^45 ≈ $105,000 at 67 (the book rounds to about $100,000).
Read it as a trade: $3,900 now costs you about $100,000 later.

4.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish cash_out(), then find what you’d actually receive cashing out a $5,000 401(k) at a 12% tax rate with the 10% penalty.

ExcelPythonR


Put the balance in A2 (5000), tax rate in B2 (0.12), and penalty in C2 (0.10). Find the cash in D2.






NoteSolution





=A2 * (1 - B2 - C2)
This returns $3,900.














Both the tax and the penalty come off the top.


def cash_out(balance, tax_rate, penalty=0.10):
    return balance * (1 - tax_rate - penalty)

cash_out(5000, 0.12)















Both the tax and the penalty come off the top.


cash_out <- function(balance, tax_rate, penalty = 0.10) {
  balance * (1 - tax_rate - penalty)
}
cash_out(5000, 0.12)









4.2 Level 2: Practice
Roll it over instead. If the $5,000 stays invested at 7% from age 22 to 67, what is it worth?

ExcelPythonR


Find the value in one formula.






NoteSolution





=5000 * 1.07^(67-22)
This returns $105,012.26.














The money grows from 22 to 67: that’s 45 years.


5000 * (1 + 0.07) ** (67 - 22)















The money grows from 22 to 67: that’s 45 years.


5000 * (1 + 0.07)^(67 - 22)









4.3 Level 3: Challenge
Three job changers at 22 cash out $2,000, $5,000, and $20,000 at a 12% tax rate with the 10% penalty. Combined, how much more would they have at 67 by rolling over (7% a year) than the cash they got?

ExcelPythonR


Put balances in A2:A4, cash now in B, value at 67 in C, and find the total difference.






NoteSolution





In B2: =A2*(1-12%-10%). In C2: =A2*1.07^45. Fill down, then =SUM(C2:C4)-SUM(B2:B4) returns $546,006.20.

















cash_out() works on a whole column. at_67 is balance * 1.07 ** 45.


changers["cash_now"] = cash_out(changers["balance"], 0.12)
changers["at_67"] = changers["balance"] * 1.07 ** 45
changers["at_67"].sum() - changers["cash_now"].sum()


















mutate(cash_now = cash_out(balance, 0.12), at_67 = balance * 1.07^45), then summarise(gap = sum(at_67) - sum(cash_now)).


changers |>
  mutate(
    cash_now = cash_out(balance, 0.12),
    at_67    = balance * 1.07^45
  ) |>
  summarise(gap = sum(at_67) - sum(cash_now)) |>
  pull(gap)

title: Taxes
text:
1 Book Topics

Where your paycheck goes: withholding for federal income tax, Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%), and state tax; FICA (7.65%) starts at the first dollar (about $3,443 on $45,000); 401(k) contributions are your money, not a tax
Tax brackets: 2026 single filer brackets (10% to 37%); only dollars above each line get the higher rate, so a raise always leaves you with more; marginal rate vs. effective rate
Deductions vs. credits: the 2026 standard deduction is $16,100; credits cut tax dollar for dollar (Saver’s Credit up to $1,000 for income up to $40,250, American Opportunity, Earned Income)
The W-4 and your refund: a big refund is an interest free loan to the government; aim for a small refund or small bill; side income needs 25% to 30% set aside for taxes (self employment tax of about 15.3%)
Filing: due around April 15; IRS Free File, VITA, Free File Fillable Forms (Direct File is not available for 2026)
Tax loss harvesting: only matters in a taxable account, and mostly delays taxes rather than avoiding them
When to hire a pro: side income, rentals or a business, big life changes, IRS letters, large taxable sales

title: Taxes
section: 2 Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
text:
2 Your Tax Bill, Bracket by Bracket
Each slice of taxable income is taxed at its own rate. The standard deduction comes off the top first, so those dollars are taxed at 0%.
Formula: Tax = Σ (Rate × Income in that bracket), and Effective rate = Tax ÷ Income





A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets







A $45,000 salary, sliced by the standard deduction and 2026 tax brackets




On $45,000, the tax is ($12,400 × 10%) + ($16,500 × 12%) = $3,220. That is an effective rate of about 7.2%, even though the top bracket is 12%.





Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer







Marginal rate (steps) vs. effective rate (smooth curve), 2026 single filer




How to read this result: the marginal rate tells you what happens to your next dollar. The effective rate tells you what share of your whole salary went to federal income tax. Use the marginal rate for decisions (like a Traditional 401(k) contribution) and the effective rate for budgeting.

2.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish income_tax() for a 2026 single filer (standard deduction $16,100), then find the federal income tax on a $45,000 salary.

ExcelPythonR


Put the salary in A2 (45000). The taxable income is the salary minus $16,100. Write the tax in B2 using the first three brackets (10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% above).






NoteSolution





=LET(t, MAX(A2-16100, 0),
  0.10*MIN(t, 12400) + 0.12*MAX(MIN(t, 50400)-12400, 0) + 0.22*MAX(MIN(t, 105700)-50400, 0))
This returns $3,220.














Taxable income is what’s left after the deduction. In each bracket, tax only the part of taxable income above that bracket’s lower edge l.


def income_tax(income, deduction=16100):
    taxable = max(income - deduction, 0)
    lower = [0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600]
    upper = lower[1:] + [float("inf")]
    rate = [0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37]
    return sum(r * max(min(taxable, u) - l, 0) for r, l, u in zip(rate, lower, upper))

income_tax(45000)















Taxable income is what’s left after the deduction. In each bracket, tax only the part of taxable income above that bracket’s lower edge.


income_tax <- function(income, deduction = 16100) {
  taxable <- max(income - deduction, 0)
  lower <- c(0, 12400, 50400, 105700, 201775, 256225, 640600)
  upper <- c(lower[-1], Inf)
  rate  <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.22, 0.24, 0.32, 0.35, 0.37)
  sum(rate * pmax(pmin(taxable, upper) - lower, 0))
}
income_tax(45000)









2.2 Level 2: Practice
What is the effective tax rate (tax ÷ income) on a $100,000 salary? Give a decimal.

ExcelPythonR


Change A2 to 100000 and divide the tax by the salary.






NoteSolution





The tax is $13,170, so =B2/A2 returns 0.1317. Even with a 22% marginal rate, only 13% of income goes to federal income tax.

















Tax on $100,000 divided by $100,000.


income_tax(100000) / 100000


















Tax on $100,000 divided by $100,000.


income_tax(100000) / 100000









2.3 Level 3: Challenge
The marginal rate is the tax on your next dollar: income_tax(salary + 1) - income_tax(salary). Checking salaries in $1,000 steps from $20,000 to $200,000, what is the lowest salary whose next dollar is taxed at 22%?

ExcelPythonR


Work it out from the brackets: the 22% bracket starts at $50,400 of taxable income.






NoteSolution





Add back the deduction: =50400 + 16100 is $66,500. The first whole $1,000 above it is $67,000.

















Use min(s for s in salaries if round(income_tax(s + 1) - income_tax(s), 2) == 0.22). Rounding avoids tiny decimal errors.


salaries = range(20000, 200001, 1000)
min(s for s in salaries if round(income_tax(s + 1) - income_tax(s), 2) == 0.22)


















income_tax() uses max(), so it handles one salary at a time. Use sapply(salaries, function(s) income_tax(s + 1) - income_tax(s)), round to 2 digits, then min(salaries[...]).


salaries <- seq(20000, 200000, by = 1000)
marginal <- sapply(salaries, function(s) income_tax(s + 1) - income_tax(s))
min(salaries[round(marginal, 2) == 0.22])

title: Taxes
section: 3 How Much of a Raise You Keep
text:
3 How Much of a Raise You Keep
The tax on a raise is the tax on the new income minus the tax on the old income. Only the part of the raise above a bracket line gets the higher rate.
Formula: Tax on raise = Tax(new income) − Tax(old income), and Amount kept = Raise − Tax on raise





A $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary that crosses into the 22% bracket







A $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary that crosses into the 22% bracket




On $66,000, taxable income goes from $49,900 to $51,900. The first $500 fills the 12% bracket and the last $1,500 is taxed at 22%. The tax rises from $5,740 to $6,130, so you keep $1,610 of the $2,000 (before FICA and state tax).
How to read this result: the share you keep can never drop below 63% (100% minus the top 37% rate). A raise that stays inside one bracket keeps exactly 1 minus that rate. A raise that crosses a line lands somewhere in between.

3.1 Level 1: Guided
Fill in the blanks to finish raise_kept(), then find how much of a $2,000 raise on a $66,000 salary you keep after federal income tax.

ExcelPythonR


With your tax formula from Level 1, put the old salary in A2 (66000) and the new salary in A3 (68000). Find the amount kept.






NoteSolution





=2000 - (B3 - B2)
The tax rises from $5,740 to $6,130, so you keep $1,610. Part of the raise is taxed at 12% and part at 22%.

















The extra tax is the tax on the new salary minus the tax on the old salary.


def raise_kept(old_income, raise_amount):
    return raise_amount - (income_tax(old_income + raise_amount) - income_tax(old_income))

raise_kept(66000, 2000)


















The extra tax is the tax on the new salary minus the tax on the old salary.


raise_kept <- function(old_income, raise) {
  raise - (income_tax(old_income + raise) - income_tax(old_income))
}
raise_kept(66000, 2000)
